source.classification: User-provided audit methodology; not official ISO text

items.title: Understanding the organization and its context
items.guidance: Verify that internal and external issues relevant to the ISMS have been determined and are kept current, including a recorded decision on whether climate change is a relevant issue (Amd 1:2024). Trace two or three listed issues into the scope, risk assessment or objectives to confirm they are actually used. ISO does not prescribe a method or format; a context register or ISMS Manual section is common.
items.intent: The organization understands the internal and external factors that could help or hinder its ISMS, and uses that understanding when planning. Amendment 1:2024 adds that the organization decides whether climate change is one of those factors.
items.verify:
Design: A method exists for identifying internal and external issues relevant to the organization's purpose and to information security.
Implementation: Issues are recorded (for example in the ISMS Manual or a context register), including a documented determination of whether climate change is relevant.
Operating effectiveness: Issues are revisited when the business changes and visibly feed the ISMS scope, risk assessment and objectives.
items.inspect:
• The current statement of internal and external issues and the date it was last reviewed
• The climate change determination and its rationale. A reasoned conclusion that it is not relevant is acceptable; no determination at all is a gap
• Trace two or three listed issues into the risk register or ISMS objectives to confirm they are actually used
• Compare the issues with changes in the last year (new services, major clients, platforms, locations, staffing) to test whether the list is current
items.questions:
• How were these issues identified, and who was involved?
• When was the context last reviewed, and what prompted the review?
• How did the organization decide whether climate change is relevant to the ISMS?
• Which significant business changes from the past year are reflected here?
• Where do these issues appear in the risk assessment?
items.evidence: ISMS Manual context section or context register; strategic or business plans; context analysis (e.g., SWOT/PESTLE); management review minutes; risk register

items.title: Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties
items.guidance: Verify relevant interested parties and their information security requirements are identified, and that the organization has decided which of those requirements the ISMS will address. Sample two or three recent client contracts, security addenda or questionnaires and confirm their requirements were captured or consciously excluded. Ask whether any climate-related expectations were considered (Amd 1:2024 note).
items.intent: The organization knows who has a stake in its information security (clients, staff, regulators, suppliers and others), what those parties expect, and which of those expectations the ISMS will take on. Amendment 1:2024 notes that such expectations can include climate-related ones.
items.verify:
Design: Relevant interested parties (clients, staff, regulators, suppliers, the certification body, insurers) and their information security requirements are identified.
Implementation: The organization has decided which requirements the ISMS addresses; legal, regulatory and contractual obligations are captured.
Operating effectiveness: The list is kept current as contracts, regulations and client expectations change, and it is used when setting scope, controls and objectives.
items.inspect:
• Interested parties register or the equivalent ISMS Manual section
• Sample two or three recent client contracts, security addenda or security questionnaires and confirm their security requirements appear, or were consciously excluded
• Evidence of the decision on which requirements the ISMS will address (made explicit in the 2022 edition)
• Links from listed requirements to the legal and contractual requirements register (A.5.31) and the SoA
items.questions:
• Who are the most important interested parties for the ISMS, and why?
• When a contract with new security obligations is signed, how do those obligations reach the ISMS?
• Which requirements did the organization decide not to address through the ISMS, and why?
• Have any interested parties raised climate-related expectations?
items.evidence: Interested parties register; client contracts, MSAs, DPAs or BAAs; security questionnaires; legal and regulatory requirements register; ISMS Manual

items.title: Determining the scope of the ISMS
items.guidance: Verify the ISMS scope is documented, approved and consistent with the certificate wording and the SoA, and that it reflects the issues, requirements, interfaces and dependencies from 4.1 and 4.2. Test it against current operations by picking a service, system or location in daily use and confirming whether it is in scope and why. The standard requires the scope to be available as documented information.
items.intent: The boundaries of the ISMS are clear and written down: what is covered, what is not and why, taking account of the context, stakeholder expectations and dependencies on other organizations.
items.verify:
Design: The scope statement identifies the organizational units, services, locations, information, technology and people covered, and justifies any exclusions.
Implementation: The scope is documented, approved and consistent with the certificate scope and the SoA.
Operating effectiveness: The scope reflects current operations; interfaces and dependencies on providers (cloud, SaaS, managed IT or security services, contractors) are understood and managed.
items.inspect:
• The approved scope statement compared with the wording on the certification certificate
• How responsibility is split with key external providers at each interface or dependency
• Test the scope against reality: pick a service, system or location in daily use and confirm whether it is in scope and why
• Any exclusions and their justification
items.questions:
• What does the ISMS cover, and what is explicitly excluded?
• Have any services, locations or platforms been added since the scope was approved?
• For key outsourced services, where does the organization's responsibility end and the provider's begin?
• Who approved the current scope, and when?
items.evidence: ISMS scope statement; certificate of registration; ISMS Manual; network and data-flow diagrams; shared-responsibility documentation; asset inventory

items.title: Information security management system
items.guidance: Verify the ISMS operates as a connected set of processes with owners, where outputs of one process feed the next (for example context into risk, risk into the SoA and objectives, audits into management review and corrective action). This clause is broad, so base the conclusion mainly on the results of the other Clause 4 to 10 items rather than testing it in isolation.
items.intent: The ISMS operates as a working management system: its processes are defined, connected to each other, kept running and improved over time.
items.verify:
Design: The ISMS processes (risk management, document control, internal audit, management review, corrective action, change, incident, supplier management and others) are defined with owners and interactions.
Implementation: Each defined process has an owner and produces the records it says it will produce.
Operating effectiveness: The processes work together: for example, audit results reach corrective action, incidents feed the risk assessment, and changes trigger document updates.
items.inspect:
• ISMS Manual or process map showing processes, owners and interactions (process interactions were made explicit in the 2022 edition)
• Pick one output (an incident, an audit result or a failed control) and trace it through each connected process to confirm the hand-offs happened
• Evidence that each core ISMS process actually ran during the audit period
items.questions:
• What are the core ISMS processes, and who owns each one?
• Give a recent example of one process's output becoming another process's input.
• Which ISMS process is weakest today, and what is being done about it?
items.evidence: ISMS Manual; process map or RACI; ISMS calendar; outputs of the risk, audit, management review and corrective action processes

items.title: Leadership and commitment
items.guidance: Interview top management to confirm they can explain the ISMS objectives, how the ISMS supports business direction, and their own part in resourcing, communicating and reviewing it. Look for observable involvement such as management review attendance, approval of policy and resources, and decisions on ISMS issues. ISO does not specify how leadership is demonstrated, so judge on actions rather than statements.
items.intent: Top management visibly owns the ISMS: it keeps security aligned with business direction, builds it into how the business operates, provides resources, explains why it matters and backs the people doing the work.
items.verify:
Design: Top management's ISMS responsibilities are defined.
Implementation: Top management takes part in ISMS decisions such as approvals, resourcing, objectives and risk acceptance.
Operating effectiveness: Commitment is visible in records across the year, not only at audit time, and ISMS requirements are embedded in business processes such as hiring, procurement, project delivery and client contracting.
items.inspect:
• Management review minutes: attendance by top management and the decisions made
• Evidence of resource decisions (budget, tools, staffing, external support)
• Leadership communications about information security
• Examples of ISMS requirements built into business processes (e.g., security review in contracting or project kickoff)
• Interview a member of top management directly, not only the ISMS lead
items.questions:
• (To top management) What is the ISMS meant to achieve, and how do you know whether it is?
• How are ISMS resource requests raised and decided? Give a recent example.
• How do you communicate the importance of information security to staff?
• Where is information security built into how the business runs day to day?
items.evidence: Management review minutes; budget and resourcing approvals; leadership communications; policy approvals; risk acceptance records; organization chart

items.title: Resources
items.guidance: Verify the resources needed for the ISMS (people, time, tools and budget) have been determined and provided. Compare planned ISMS activities such as audits, risk reviews, training and remediation with what was actually delivered, and ask whether any were delayed or dropped for lack of resources.
items.intent: The ISMS has the people, budget, tools and support it needs to run and improve.
items.verify:
Design: Resource needs for the ISMS (people, budget, tools, external support) are identified.
Implementation: Resources are provided: budget approved, roles staffed, tools licensed, support contracted.
Operating effectiveness: Resources are adequate in practice; chronic backlogs, overdue actions or missed objectives caused by resource gaps are escalated and addressed.
items.inspect:
• Budget and resourcing decisions for ISMS activities
• Staffing of ISMS roles and any single-person dependencies
• Overdue risk treatments, audits or corrective actions attributed to resource constraints
• Management review outputs on resource needs
items.questions:
• How are ISMS resource needs identified and requested?
• Were any requests declined or deferred, and what was the impact?
• Does the ISMS depend on one person? Who covers if they are unavailable?
items.evidence: Budget records; management review outputs; contracts for external support; staffing plans; tool licensing

items.title: Information security policy
items.guidance: Review the current information security policy for top management approval, a current review date, and the commitments and objectives framework the standard expects. Confirm staff can locate it and that it has been communicated internally and made available to interested parties as appropriate. The standard requires the policy to be available as documented information.
items.intent: A top-level information security policy set by top management fits the business, frames the objectives and commits the organization to meeting its obligations and to improving. It is documented, communicated internally and shared with interested parties where appropriate.
items.verify:
Design: The policy is appropriate to the organization and the ISMS, provides a framework for setting objectives, and contains the required commitments to satisfy applicable requirements and to continually improve.
Implementation: The policy is approved by top management, current, communicated within the organization, and available to interested parties as appropriate.
Operating effectiveness: Policy requirements are reflected in how the ISMS actually runs, and the policy remains appropriate to the organization's purpose. Review at planned intervals and after significant change is an A.5.1 requirement and is tested there.
items.inspect:
• The approved Information Security Policy and evidence of top management approval
• Current version, review date and version history
• Documented communication to staff (acknowledgements, onboarding, announcements)
• Availability to relevant interested parties where appropriate (e.g., on request by clients)
• Confirm the commitments to meet applicable requirements and to continual improvement are present
• Compare two or three policy statements with actual practice to test that the policy is reflected in the ISMS
items.questions:
• Who approves the policy?
• When was it last reviewed?
• How are changes communicated?
• How does management ensure the policy remains appropriate?
items.evidence: Information Security Policy; approval record; policy acknowledgement reports; policy location on the controlled document repository or intranet; document version history

items.title: Policies for information security
items.guidance: Review the list of topic-specific policies and sample several for management approval, a current review date, and evidence of review after significant change. Check acknowledgement records for a sample of staff and contractors and confirm policies are easy to find. Which topic-specific policies are needed is the organization's decision.
items.intent: Management has set clear security rules for the organization; people know the rules exist, have acknowledged them and can rely on them being kept current.
items.verify:
Design: A policy set covers the topics the organization needs (e.g., access control, acceptable use, backup, cryptography, incident management, supplier security), each with an owner and a review frequency.
Implementation: Policies are approved at the right management level, published where people can find them, and acknowledged by relevant personnel.
Operating effectiveness: Policies are reviewed on schedule and after significant change, and their content matches actual practice.
items.inspect:
• Policy library index: owner, approval date and last review date against the required review frequency
• Acknowledgement records for a sample of recent hires and long-standing staff
• Pick two or three specific policy statements and check them against practice (e.g., a stated password or retention rule against the actual configuration)
• Evidence of policy review after a significant change (new platform, reorganization, incident)
items.questions:
• Which topic-specific policies exist, and who owns each?
• How are staff told about new or changed policies?
• When was the last policy review cycle completed?
• Is there any policy statement the organization knows it does not currently meet?
items.evidence: Policy library on the controlled document repository; approval records; acknowledgement reports (HR system or training platform); policy review schedule
items.guidance_notes: Clause 5.2 covers the top-level policy; this control covers the full policy set.

items.title: Organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities
items.guidance: Compare the documented ISMS role assignments (for example in the ISMS Manual, a RACI or job descriptions) with who actually does the work, including who reports ISMS performance to top management. Interview one or two role holders to confirm they understand their responsibilities and authority and know how they were assigned.
items.intent: Everyone with an ISMS role knows their responsibilities and authority, and specific people are accountable for keeping the ISMS conformant and for reporting its performance to top management.
items.verify:
Design: ISMS roles, responsibilities and authorities are defined, including conformity and performance-reporting responsibilities.
Implementation: Roles are assigned to named people and communicated to them.
Operating effectiveness: Role holders understand and perform their responsibilities, and ISMS performance is actually reported to top management.
items.inspect:
• Role definitions (ISMS Manual, RACI, job descriptions) and the named assignments
• Evidence of ISMS performance reporting to top management (reports, meeting records)
• Interview two or three role holders to confirm they know their responsibilities
• Check that assignments survived staff changes (no departed employees still named)
items.questions:
• Who is accountable for the ISMS conforming to ISO/IEC 27001?
• Who reports ISMS performance to top management, how often, and in what form?
• How were you told about your ISMS responsibilities?
• What happens to your ISMS responsibilities when you are unavailable?
items.evidence: ISMS Manual roles section; RACI; job descriptions; appointment emails or letters; organization chart; ISMS performance reports

items.title: Information security roles and responsibilities
items.guidance: Verify operational security responsibilities, such as asset owners, risk owners, access approvers and incident handlers, are defined and allocated to named roles or people. Interview two or three role holders to confirm they know and perform these responsibilities, and check allocations were updated after recent staff changes.
items.intent: Every security activity has an owner, so nothing important falls between the cracks, including activities performed by providers.
items.verify:
Design: Operational security roles are defined (asset owners, risk owners, system administrators, incident handlers, supplier relationship owners).
Implementation: Each role is allocated to a named person, including responsibilities performed by external providers.
Operating effectiveness: Role holders perform their responsibilities, and gaps caused by staff turnover are filled promptly.
items.inspect:
• RACI or roles matrix for security activities, including responsibilities held by external providers (e.g., a managed IT or security provider)
• Named owners in the asset inventory and risk register: confirm they are current employees
• Interview two role holders about what they are responsible for
items.questions:
• Who is responsible for [a specific activity, e.g., reviewing firewall rules or running access reviews]?
• Which security responsibilities sit with external providers, and where is that written down?
• How are responsibilities reassigned when someone leaves?
items.evidence: Roles or RACI matrix; job descriptions; asset inventory owner fields; risk register owner fields; provider contracts and statements of work
items.guidance_notes: Clause 5.3 covers ISMS management roles; this control covers operational security roles.

items.title: Segregation of duties
items.guidance: Identify conflicting duties in key processes, such as requesting and approving access, writing and deploying code, or raising and approving changes, and verify they are separated. Where team size prevents separation, confirm compensating controls such as independent review or activity logging are defined and operating.
items.intent: No single person can carry out, approve and conceal a sensitive action alone, which reduces the chance of fraud, error or bypassed controls.
items.verify:
Design: Conflicting combinations of duties are identified (e.g., requesting and approving access, writing and deploying production code, administering systems and reviewing their logs).
Implementation: Conflicts are separated through role design and system permissions; where full separation is not feasible, compensating controls such as independent review or monitoring exist.
Operating effectiveness: Separation holds in practice, and exceptions are reviewed.
items.inspect:
• Documented conflicting-duty combinations and any compensating controls
• Sample access requests: requester and approver are different people
• Sample production changes: author and approver differ, or a documented compensating review exists
• Administrators who can alter or delete logs of their own activity
items.questions:
• Which activities should never be performed end to end by one person here?
• In a small team, where is separation not possible, and what compensates?
• Can anyone approve their own access request or their own change?
items.evidence: Segregation of duties matrix; access request tickets; change records; repository branch protection and approval settings; admin role assignments; log access permissions

items.title: Management responsibilities
items.guidance: Verify managers require staff and contractors to follow security policies and procedures, for example through onboarding, team briefings, performance expectations and support for training. Interview one or two line managers about how they reinforce security expectations and handle non-compliance in their teams.
items.intent: Managers make sure their people actually follow the organization's security rules, rather than leaving security to the IT or security team.
items.verify:
Design: Managers' security responsibilities are defined (ensuring training is completed, policy is followed and incidents are reported).
Implementation: Managers act on those responsibilities, for example following up overdue training and approving access for their team.
Operating effectiveness: Staff behavior reflects management expectations, and managers address noncompliance.
items.inspect:
• Evidence that managers follow up overdue training or policy acknowledgement
• Manager involvement in access reviews and in joiner, mover and leaver requests
• Examples of management addressing policy noncompliance
• Interview a line manager outside IT and security
items.questions:
• (To a line manager) What are your information security responsibilities for your team?
• How do you know whether your team has completed required training?
• What would you do if a team member kept ignoring a security requirement?
items.evidence: Training completion reports by manager; access review sign-offs; onboarding and offboarding tickets; management communications

items.title: Actions to address risks and opportunities (general)
items.guidance: Verify that ISMS-related risks and opportunities are identified and that appropriate actions are planned, assigned, implemented, and evaluated for effectiveness. Review the risk register, related action tracking, management review information, or other evidence demonstrating identified risks and opportunities are being addressed.
items.intent: When planning the ISMS, the organization anticipates what could stop the ISMS from working and what could make it work better, then plans and follows up actions. This concerns the management system itself and is separate from the information security risk assessment in 6.1.2.
items.verify:
Design: There is a way to identify ISMS-level risks and opportunities, such as key-person dependency, resource constraints or scope growth, based on the context and interested party requirements.
Implementation: Planned actions exist and are integrated into ISMS processes.
Operating effectiveness: Actions are carried out and their effectiveness is evaluated.
items.inspect:
• Record of ISMS-level risks and opportunities (may sit in the risk register or ISMS Manual)
• Traceability from 4.1 issues and 4.2 requirements to these risks and opportunities
• Action plans with owners and dates
• Evidence that effectiveness was evaluated, for example in management review
items.questions:
• What could stop the ISMS itself from achieving its outcomes?
• What opportunities for improving the ISMS have been identified?
• How do you know whether the planned actions worked?
items.evidence: Risk and opportunity register; ISMS Manual; action plans; management review minutes

items.title: Information security risk assessment (process)
items.guidance: Verify the organization has a defined and repeatable information security risk assessment process with established risk criteria, likelihood/impact methodology, risk ownership, and documented results. Confirm assessments are performed consistently and retained as evidence.
items.intent: Information security risks are assessed with a defined, repeatable method: agreed criteria for assessing and accepting risk, identified risks to confidentiality, integrity and availability, named risk owners, and ratings that allow risks to be compared and prioritized.
items.verify:
Design: The methodology defines acceptance criteria, when assessments are performed, and likelihood and consequence scales that make results repeatable.
Implementation: The risk register records CIA risks with named risk owners, analyzed and evaluated per the methodology, and the process is retained as documented information.
Operating effectiveness: The methodology is applied consistently, so a different assessor would reach similar ratings, and the register is kept current.
items.inspect:
• Risk methodology: acceptance criteria, likelihood and consequence scales, definition of risk owner
• Sample five to eight risks and re-perform the scoring against the methodology to test consistency
• Each sampled risk has an owner with the accountability and authority to manage it; where a department or group is named, confirm who exercises that accountability in practice (naming an individual or role is good practice)
• Coverage: do risks address key assets, services, suppliers and the issues from 4.1?
• Look for risks that clearly exist in operations but are missing from the register
items.questions:
• Walk me through how a new risk is identified, scored and recorded.
• What is the risk acceptance threshold, and who set it?
• Do the named risk owners know they own these risks?
• How do you make sure two people would score the same risk similarly?
• Which risks changed rating in the last assessment, and why?
items.evidence: Risk Management Policy and methodology; risk register; risk assessment reports; risk workshop notes; asset inventory; threat intelligence inputs

items.title: Information security risk assessment (performance)
items.guidance: Verify risk assessments were performed at the planned intervals and when significant changes occurred or were proposed, using the 6.1.2 method. Review the latest results for date and approval, and check whether significant changes in the past year (new services, platforms, suppliers or client obligations) triggered a reassessment. The standard requires assessment results to be retained as documented information.
items.intent: Risk assessments are actually carried out on the planned schedule and whenever significant change calls for one, and the results are kept.
items.verify:
Design: The planned interval and the triggers for reassessment are defined.
Implementation: Assessments were performed at the planned interval during the audit period.
Operating effectiveness: Significant changes triggered reassessment, and results are retained.
items.inspect:
• Dates of risk assessments compared with the defined interval
• Significant changes in the period (new systems, services, suppliers, incidents) and whether each triggered a reassessment
• Retained assessment results
items.questions:
• When was the last full risk assessment?
• Which changes triggered an out-of-cycle assessment this year?
• Where are the results kept?
items.evidence: Risk assessment reports; risk register history; change records; project risk assessments

items.title: Information security risk treatment (process and plan)
items.area: Risk treatment and Statement of Applicability
items.guidance: Verify the risk treatment process selects treatment options, determines the controls needed, compares them with Annex A, and produces a treatment plan that risk owners have approved, including acceptance of residual risk. Trace two or three high risks from the register into the treatment plan and confirm the chosen controls exist in practice. The standard requires documented information about the treatment process to be retained.
items.intent: Risks above the acceptance criteria are treated deliberately: treatment options and controls are chosen, checked against Annex A so nothing needed is missed, set out in a treatment plan and approved by risk owners, who also accept the risk that remains.
items.verify:
Design: Treatment options and controls are selected for risks above the acceptance criteria, and the risk treatment plan defines actions, owners and timing.
Implementation: Risk owners have approved the treatment plan and formally accepted residual risks.
Operating effectiveness: The plan is progressing, the selected controls exist in practice, and accepted risks are re-evaluated when circumstances change.
items.inspect:
• Risk treatment plan: actions, owners, target dates and status
• Evidence of risk owner approval of the plan and acceptance of residual risk (signature, email, minutes, GRC record)
• Sample three to five treated risks and confirm the selected control is actually in place (cross-check with Annex A audit results)
• Overdue treatment actions and how they are being managed
items.questions:
• How is a treatment option chosen (reduce, avoid, transfer or accept)?
• Who can accept residual risk, and how is that acceptance recorded?
• Which treatment actions are overdue, and what is the plan for them?
• How was Annex A used to check that no necessary control was missed?
items.evidence: Risk treatment plan; risk register treatment fields; risk acceptance records; project or ticket records for treatment actions; Statement of Applicability

items.title: Information security risk treatment (implementation)
items.area: Risk treatment and Statement of Applicability
items.guidance: Verify the risk treatment plan is being implemented. Sample several planned treatments and confirm the controls are in place or the actions are tracked with owners and dates, and that overdue actions are escalated. The standard requires the results of risk treatment to be retained as documented information.
items.intent: The risk treatment plan is actually carried out, and the results are kept.
items.verify:
Design: The treatment plan from 6.1.3 defines what will be implemented.
Implementation: Treatment actions are being implemented as planned.
Operating effectiveness: Results are retained, completed treatments reduced risk as intended, and residual risk ratings were updated.
items.inspect:
• Status of treatment plan actions
• Sample three completed actions and verify the control is in place
• Overdue actions and their reasons
• Residual risk ratings updated after completion
items.questions:
• Which risk treatment actions were completed this period?
• How was the effect on the risk level evaluated after completion?
• What is blocking the overdue actions?
items.evidence: Risk treatment plan status; tickets or project records; risk register residual ratings; evidence of implemented controls

items.title: Statement of Applicability
items.area: Risk treatment and Statement of Applicability
items.guidance: Verify the Statement of Applicability is current and approved, gives a justification for each Annex A control's inclusion and its implementation status, and aligns with the risk treatment plan. Reconcile the SoA with the Applicability column in these worksheets and sample several controls to check the stated implementation status is accurate.
items.intent: The Statement of Applicability records, for every Annex A control, whether it is needed and why, and whether it is in place, and it includes any additional controls the organization relies on.
items.verify:
Design: The SoA addresses all 93 Annex A controls plus any additional controls, with inclusion or exclusion justification and implementation status.
Implementation: The SoA is approved, current, version controlled and consistent with the risk treatment plan.
Operating effectiveness: The SoA is updated when risks, scope or controls change; exclusions remain justified; implementation status is accurate.
items.inspect:
• Current approved SoA: version, date and approver
• Every Annex A control is addressed with a justification
• Test two or three exclusions against actual operations (e.g., an exclusion for development while code is being written)
• Test three to five 'implemented' claims against reality or against results from the other audits
• Reconcile the SoA with the Applicability column in the quarterly worksheets
items.questions:
• When was the SoA last updated, and what triggered the change?
• Who approves the SoA?
• How are controls linked back to the risks they treat?
• Which controls are partially implemented or planned, and when will they be complete?
items.evidence: Statement of Applicability; SoA approval record; risk treatment plan; risk register; certificate scope

items.title: Information security objectives and planning to achieve them
items.guidance: Verify objectives are consistent with the policy, measurable where practicable, monitored and communicated, and that each has a plan showing what will be done, by whom, by when and how results will be evaluated. Check that objectives are kept distinct from the one-time actions planned to achieve them. The standard requires documented information on objectives to be retained.
items.intent: Information security objectives follow from the policy, are measurable where practicable and reflect requirements and risk results. Each has a plan covering what will be done, by whom, with what resources, by when and how results will be judged.
items.verify:
Design: Objectives are consistent with the policy, measurable where practicable, and reflect applicable requirements and risk assessment results.
Implementation: Each objective has planned actions, resources, an owner, a timeframe and an evaluation method.
Operating effectiveness: Objectives are monitored, reported, communicated and updated, and results are evaluated.
items.inspect:
• Objectives register: test each objective for a metric, target and timeframe
• Distinguish objectives (results to be achieved, measurable where practicable) from the actions planned to achieve them; one-time implementation tasks belong in the plan for an objective, not in place of one
• Evidence of monitoring over time (metric values) and reporting to management
• Communication of objectives to the people responsible for them
• Evidence that objectives were revised when circumstances changed
items.questions:
• How is progress against each objective measured, and where is it reported?
• Which objectives were met or missed last period, and what happened as a result?
• How were these objectives chosen, and how do they relate to the risk assessment?
• Who owns each objective?
items.evidence: ISMS Objectives Register; KPI or metrics reports; management review minutes; communications to staff

items.title: Planning of changes
items.guidance: Identify ISMS changes made since the last audit, such as scope, roles, key systems, suppliers or processes, and verify they were planned and carried out in a controlled way rather than ad hoc. The standard does not prescribe a change-planning method or require documented information here, so accept any reasonable approach the organization applies consistently.
items.intent: Changes to the ISMS itself are planned before they are made rather than made ad hoc. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: There is a defined way to plan changes to the management system itself (scope changes, new or retired processes, reorganizations, provider changes affecting the ISMS).
Implementation: Significant ISMS changes in the period show evidence of planning before they were carried out. ISO/IEC 27001 does not prescribe what the planning must cover; considering purpose, potential consequences, resources and responsibilities is good practice.
Operating effectiveness: Changes did not undermine the ISMS; affected documents, risk assessments and the SoA were updated afterwards.
items.inspect:
• Identify significant ISMS changes in the audit period and look for planning evidence for each
• Confirm that documents, risk assessments and the SoA were updated after each change
• Keep this distinct from technical change management (A.8.32); this clause concerns the management system
items.questions:
• What significant changes were made to the ISMS in the past year?
• How was each change planned, and who approved it?
• What had to be updated as a result?
items.evidence: ISMS change records; project plans; management review minutes; document version histories; risk register updates

items.title: Documented information (general)
items.guidance: Verify the ISMS holds the documented information the standard explicitly requires and the additional documentation the organization has decided it needs for the ISMS to be effective. Check each required item exists and is current. How much additional documentation to keep is the organization's decision, so test against its own determination.
items.intent: The ISMS has the documentation ISO/IEC 27001 calls for, plus whatever else the organization has decided it needs for the ISMS to work.
items.verify:
Design: The organization knows which documented information the standard requires and which additional documents it needs.
Implementation: That documented information exists and is current.
Operating effectiveness: Documentation is proportionate and actually used by the people it is written for.
items.inspect:
• Document register or master list of ISMS documents
• Confirm the required items exist: scope (4.3), policy (5.2), risk assessment and treatment processes (6.1.2, 6.1.3), SoA, objectives (6.2), competence evidence (7.2), operational planning records (8.1), risk assessment and treatment results (8.2, 8.3), monitoring results (9.1), audit program and results (9.2), management review results (9.3), nonconformities and corrective actions (10.2)
• Documents that exist but no one uses
items.questions:
• Where is the master list of ISMS documents?
• How did you decide which additional documents the ISMS needs?
• Which documents are rarely used, and why?
items.evidence: Document register; the controlled document repository document library; ISMS Manual

items.title: Creating and updating documented information
items.guidance: Sample several ISMS documents and verify each has appropriate identification (title, owner, version, date), a suitable format, and evidence of review and approval before issue. Check that two or three recently changed documents followed the same review and approval path.
items.intent: ISMS documents can be identified (title, date, author or reference), are in a suitable format, and are checked and approved before use.
items.verify:
Design: Document standards define identification, format and review and approval requirements.
Implementation: Documents carry title, version, date, owner and approval.
Operating effectiveness: Updates follow the process, and approval happens before publication.
items.inspect:
• Sample five ISMS documents: document control table, version history and approval evidence
• Review dates compared with the required review frequency
• Drafts versus published versions, and who approved the published version
items.questions:
• Who can approve a new version of a policy?
• How often must documents be reviewed, and how is that tracked?
• How are staff told when an important document changes?
items.evidence: Document control tables; version histories; the controlled document repository version history; approval emails or workflows

items.title: Control of documented information
items.guidance: Verify documented information is available where needed and protected against loss, unauthorized change and unintended use of obsolete versions. In the controlled document repository, check permissions on ISMS libraries, version history on a changed document, and retention or disposal settings. Confirm how external documents, such as client or supplier documents, are identified and controlled.
items.intent: ISMS documents and records reach the people who need them, are protected from misuse and loss, are version controlled, and are retained and disposed of properly. Documents from outside sources that the ISMS relies on are also controlled.
items.verify:
Design: Rules exist for access, distribution, storage, retention and disposal of ISMS documents and records.
Implementation: Controlled documents live in approved locations with appropriate permissions, and external documents are identified.
Operating effectiveness: People use current versions, obsolete versions are withdrawn or marked, and records are kept for the required period.
items.inspect:
• Permissions on the ISMS the controlled document repository libraries (who can edit versus read)
• Uncontrolled copies in circulation (emailed PDFs, local copies, outdated versions on shared drives)
• List of external-origin documents (standards, regulations, client requirements, vendor guidance)
• Retention settings and handling of obsolete versions
items.questions:
• How do you make sure people are using the current version?
• Who can edit the ISMS document library?
• How are records protected from alteration or deletion?
• How are external documents such as standards or client requirements tracked?
items.evidence: the controlled document repository library permissions and version history; retention labels or policies; document register; external documents list

items.title: Documented operating procedures
items.guidance: Verify operating procedures exist for key information processing activities and are available to the people who need them. Sample two or three procedures, such as backup, onboarding or deployment, and compare them with how the task is actually performed; outdated procedures are a common finding.
items.intent: Key operational tasks are written down clearly enough that the people who need to perform them can do so consistently.
items.verify:
Design: Procedures exist for key operational activities (backup and restore, user provisioning, patching, system builds, incident handling, deployments).
Implementation: Procedures are available to the people who need them, including backup staff and external providers.
Operating effectiveness: Procedures are current and followed, so someone other than the usual person can perform the task consistently.
items.inspect:
• Index of operating procedures and runbooks with last review dates
• Choose two procedures and compare them with how the task is actually done (walkthrough)
• Availability to on-call or backup staff
items.questions:
• If the person who usually does this task were unavailable, how would someone else do it?
• When was this procedure last updated?
• Where does the procedure differ from how the task is really done?
items.evidence: Runbooks and SOPs; IT knowledge base or documentation platform; the controlled document repository procedures library; change records that reference procedures

items.title: Protection of records
items.guidance: Verify records are protected from loss, destruction, falsification and unauthorized access or release, in line with retention requirements. Sample several record types, such as HR, financial, audit or client records, and confirm retention periods are defined and applied and that access and deletion are controlled.
items.intent: Records the organization must keep survive intact and confidential for as long as they are needed, and are then disposed of properly.
items.verify:
Design: A retention schedule defines record types, retention periods, storage and protection requirements based on legal and contractual needs.
Implementation: Records are stored with appropriate protection (access control, immutability, backup) and retention settings are configured.
Operating effectiveness: Records are kept and disposed of on schedule, and their integrity is preserved.
items.inspect:
• Records retention schedule
• Retention configuration in key systems (Microsoft 365 retention policies, email archiving, ticketing, HR and finance systems)
• Sample record types: available for the required period and protected from alteration
• Disposal records at end of retention
items.questions:
• Which records must be kept, and for how long?
• How are records protected from deletion or alteration?
• How is expired information disposed of?
items.evidence: Data Retention and Disposal Policy and schedule; retention policy configuration; archive settings; disposal logs

items.title: Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements
items.guidance: Verify legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements relevant to information security are identified, kept up to date, and linked to how the organization meets them. Sample two or three obligations, such as a client contract clause or privacy requirement, and trace each to the controls that address it. Confirm who monitors for changes.
items.intent: The organization knows which laws, regulations and contracts place security obligations on it, keeps that knowledge current and knows how it meets each obligation.
items.verify:
Design: A register of applicable requirements exists (privacy and data protection, breach notification, sector rules, export controls, contractual obligations), with owners.
Implementation: Requirements are mapped to the policies and controls that meet them.
Operating effectiveness: The register is kept current as laws change and contracts are signed, and compliance is monitored.
items.inspect:
• Legal and contractual requirements register: last update date and owner
• Sample two recent client contracts: are their security obligations captured?
• How changes in law are monitored (counsel updates, subscriptions)
• Requirements relating to the use, import or export of cryptography where relevant
items.questions:
• Which laws and regulations most affect information security here?
• How are security obligations in new client contracts captured and passed to the people who must meet them?
• Who monitors changes in applicable law?
items.evidence: Legal and regulatory requirements register; client contracts; legal counsel advice; privacy notices; compliance calendar

items.title: Privacy and protection of PII
items.guidance: Verify the privacy and PII protection requirements that apply to the organization are identified and met, including its role as controller or processor for client data. Sample one or two processing activities or client data sets and confirm required protections, agreements and handling rules are in place. Confirm with the privacy or legal owner which requirements apply rather than assuming.
items.intent: Personal information is handled in line with the privacy laws, regulations and contracts that apply to it.
items.verify:
Design: Privacy requirements are identified (laws, client contracts, DPAs or BAAs), and privacy responsibilities are assigned.
Implementation: PII processing is known (what PII, where, why, for whom), and privacy controls such as access restriction, minimization and retention are implemented.
Operating effectiveness: Privacy incidents and requests are handled, and controls operate as intended.
items.inspect:
• Data inventory or record of processing for PII, including PII processed on behalf of clients
• Privacy notice and contractual privacy obligations
• Sample a PII repository: access restricted and retention applied
• Privacy incidents or requests in the period
items.questions:
• What personal information does the organization process, including on behalf of clients?
• Who is responsible for privacy compliance?
• How are client obligations for personal data tracked and met?
items.evidence: Data inventory or record of processing; privacy notice; DPAs and BAAs; access reports for PII repositories; privacy request log

items.title: Intellectual property rights
items.guidance: Verify procedures protect intellectual property rights, including software licensing, open-source components, and third-party data or models. Compare a sample of installed software or subscriptions with license records, and confirm how open-source license obligations are checked during development.
items.intent: The organization respects intellectual property: it uses properly licensed software and third-party material and protects proprietary and client-owned work.
items.verify:
Design: Rules cover software licensing, use of third-party and open-source code, and handling of client and proprietary IP.
Implementation: Software licenses are tracked, and open-source license obligations are managed where software is developed.
Operating effectiveness: License checks show no unlicensed software, and contractual IP obligations are respected.
items.inspect:
• Software license records compared with installed software (sample from the RMM software inventory)
• Open-source license review in development, if applicable
• Handling of client IP and deliverables under contract terms
items.questions:
• How do you make sure installed software is properly licensed?
• How are open-source license obligations checked before a library is used?
• How is client-owned IP protected and returned when a contract ends?
items.evidence: License management records; RMM software inventory; procurement records; open-source license scan results; contract IP clauses

items.title: Screening
items.guidance: Sample recent hires and contractors and verify background checks were completed before joining, and on an ongoing basis where the policy requires, in line with the organization's screening policy and proportionate to role and access. Confirm how screening is handled for contractors supplied by third parties. Screening depth is set by the organization within local law, so test against its own policy.
items.intent: People are checked before they are given access, to a depth that matches the role, the information involved and applicable law.
items.verify:
Design: Screening requirements are defined by role and risk, consistent with law and client contractual requirements.
Implementation: Screening was completed before access was granted for sampled hires, including contractors where required.
Operating effectiveness: Exceptions are approved, and re-screening happens where required (e.g., moving into a privileged role or a client requirement).
items.inspect:
• Screening requirements by role
• Sample three to five recent hires or contractors: screening completion date compared with start date and system access date. Confirm completion status only; do not review the screening results themselves
• Client contractual screening requirements and how they are met
items.questions:
• What checks are performed before someone starts?
• What happens if screening is not complete by the start date?
• Are contractors screened, by whom, and how do you know?
items.evidence: HR onboarding records; screening provider completion status reports; contractor agreements; client contract screening clauses

items.title: Terms and conditions of employment
items.guidance: Verify employment contracts and contractor agreements state information security responsibilities, and that current templates reflect current policy. Sample several recent contracts or agreements and confirm the relevant clauses are present and signed.
items.intent: Employment and contractor terms make security responsibilities clear from the outset.
items.verify:
Design: Employment agreements and contractor agreements include security responsibilities (confidentiality, acceptable use, IP, obligations after leaving).
Implementation: Sampled personnel have signed agreements containing those terms.
Operating effectiveness: Templates are current and consistent with policy.
items.inspect:
• Offer letter, employment agreement and contractor agreement templates
• Sample signed agreements for employees and contractors
• Date the templates were last reviewed
items.questions:
• Where are security responsibilities stated in employment terms?
• How are contractor terms handled?
• When were the templates last reviewed against current policy?
items.evidence: Offer letter and contract templates; signed agreements in the HR system; contractor agreements; employee handbook

items.title: Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements
items.guidance: Verify confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements reflect the organization's protection needs, are signed by employees, contractors and relevant external parties, and are reviewed periodically. Sample several people with access to client or sensitive information and confirm a current signed agreement exists.
items.intent: People and organizations given confidential information have signed agreements that protect it, and those agreements stay fit for purpose.
items.verify:
Design: NDA requirements are defined (who must sign, what terms, for how long), and templates are reviewed periodically.
Implementation: Signed NDAs exist for sampled employees, contractors and third parties with access to confidential information.
Operating effectiveness: NDA terms are updated when requirements change, such as new client confidentiality obligations.
items.inspect:
• NDA templates and date of last review
• Sample signed NDAs for employees, contractors and third parties
• Client-required confidentiality terms flowed down to contractors
items.questions:
• Who must sign an NDA before receiving confidential information?
• When were the NDA templates last reviewed?
• How are client confidentiality obligations passed on to contractors?
items.evidence: NDA templates; signed NDAs; contractor and supplier agreements; contract management records

items.title: Disciplinary process
items.guidance: Verify a disciplinary process for security policy violations is defined and communicated so staff understand the consequences. Confirm with HR how the process applies to security breaches; the auditor needs to confirm the process exists and is known, not review individual cases.
items.intent: There are known, fair consequences for violating security policy, and they are applied consistently.
items.verify:
Design: The disciplinary process covers security policy violations and is proportionate.
Implementation: The process is communicated through the handbook, acceptable use rules or training.
Operating effectiveness: The process is applied consistently when violations occur.
items.inspect:
• HR handbook or disciplinary policy wording on security violations
• Evidence the process is communicated to staff
• Confirm with HR, at summary level only, whether the process has been applied to a security violation
items.questions:
• How are staff told about the consequences of policy violations?
• Has the process been applied to a security violation? (Summary only; no personal details.)
• Who decides the response?
items.evidence: Employee handbook; disciplinary policy; Acceptable Use Policy; aggregate HR case summary

items.title: Responsibilities after termination or change of employment
items.guidance: Verify security responsibilities that continue after termination or change of role, such as confidentiality, are defined, communicated and enforced. Sample recent leavers and confirm exit communications or agreements reminded them of their continuing obligations.
items.intent: Security obligations that outlast employment or a role change are defined, communicated and enforced.
items.verify:
Design: Continuing obligations (confidentiality, IP, return or deletion of data) are defined in agreements.
Implementation: Leavers are reminded of their obligations at exit, and role changes trigger updates to access and responsibilities.
Operating effectiveness: Obligations are enforced if they are breached.
items.inspect:
• Exit checklist includes a reminder of ongoing confidentiality obligations
• Sample three leavers for evidence of that reminder
• Role change process for moves into and out of privileged roles
items.questions:
• How are leavers reminded of their ongoing confidentiality obligations?
• What changes when someone moves into or out of a privileged role?
items.evidence: Exit checklist; offboarding tickets; employment and contractor agreements

items.title: Competence
items.guidance: Verify the competence needed for roles that affect information security has been defined and that role holders meet it through education, training or experience. Sample several people in security-relevant roles, including internal auditors, and confirm records support their competence and that any gaps were addressed and the action evaluated. The standard requires competence evidence to be retained as documented information.
items.intent: People whose work affects information security are capable of doing it: the organization knows what each role needs, closes gaps, checks that its actions worked and keeps evidence.
items.verify:
Design: Competence requirements are defined for ISMS-relevant roles (security, system administration, development, risk owners, internal auditors).
Implementation: People in those roles meet the requirements, or actions such as training, mentoring or hiring are under way.
Operating effectiveness: The effectiveness of competence actions is evaluated, and evidence is retained and current.
items.inspect:
• Competence requirements for three or four key roles, including internal auditors
• Sample individuals and compare their training, certifications or experience with the requirement
• Evidence that effectiveness of training was evaluated (assessment, supervisor review, observed performance)
• Competence evidence for the internal auditors (ISO/IEC 27001 knowledge and audit technique)
items.questions:
• What competence is required to administer critical systems here?
• How do you know training actually improved competence?
• What qualifies the internal auditors to audit the ISMS?
items.evidence: Job descriptions; skills matrix; training records; certifications; HR records; auditor qualification records

items.title: Awareness
items.guidance: Interview a sample of staff across functions to confirm they know the information security policy exists, how their work contributes to the ISMS, and what happens if requirements are not followed. Awareness is tested through conversation; training completion records (A.6.3) support the conclusion but do not prove it on their own.
items.intent: People working for the organization understand the security policy, how their own work contributes to the ISMS and what follows if they do not meet its requirements.
items.verify:
Design: The awareness program covers the policy, each person's contribution and the consequences of nonconformity. A.6.3 covers the wider awareness, education and training program, including role-based training.
Implementation: All in-scope personnel, including contractors, receive awareness.
Operating effectiveness: People can actually explain the policy basics, how to report an incident and what is expected of them.
items.inspect:
• Awareness content and completion records compared with the current staff and contractor list
• Interview three to five people outside IT and security about where the policy is, how to report an incident and their responsibilities
• Phishing simulation or knowledge-check results if used
items.questions:
• (To staff) Where would you find the information security policy?
• What would you do if you clicked a suspicious link or thought your account was compromised?
• What information security responsibilities apply to your role?
• What could happen if someone ignored the policy?
items.evidence: Awareness platform reports; policy acknowledgements; onboarding checklist; phishing simulation reports; staff and contractor roster

items.title: Information security awareness, education and training
items.guidance: Verify security awareness, education and training is provided at onboarding and periodically, is relevant to roles, and is updated when policies or threats change. Sample completion records for several staff, including role-specific training for technical or privileged users, and confirm how non-completion is followed up.
items.intent: People receive security awareness, education and training suited to their role, and are kept up to date as policies and threats change.
items.verify:
Design: The training program defines content by audience (all staff, developers, administrators, privileged users, executives), frequency and completion expectations.
Implementation: Training is delivered and completion is tracked, including for new hires within a defined timeframe.
Operating effectiveness: Completion meets the target, overdue training is escalated, effectiveness is measured and content is refreshed for current threats.
items.inspect:
• Training plan and role-based content
• Completion reports compared with current headcount, and follow-up of overdue training
• New hire completion within the required window (sample three)
• Phishing simulation or knowledge-check trends
items.questions:
• What training does a developer or administrator receive beyond general awareness?
• What happens when someone does not complete training?
• How do you know training is changing behavior?
items.evidence: Security Awareness and Training Policy; training platform reports; phishing simulation reports; onboarding checklists

items.title: Communication
items.guidance: Verify the organization has decided which ISMS communications are needed internally and externally, covering what, when, with whom, who communicates and how. Sample two or three recent communications, such as a policy update, incident notice or client security communication, and confirm they followed that approach. ISO does not require a separate communication plan document.
items.intent: The organization has decided which ISMS matters need communicating, to whom, when and by what means, both internally and externally.
items.verify:
Design: A communication plan or matrix sets out what is communicated, when, with whom and how.
Implementation: Planned communications take place.
Operating effectiveness: Communications reach the intended audiences, including external parties such as clients, regulators and the certification body when required.
items.inspect:
• Communication plan or matrix
• Sample three planned communications and confirm they occurred
• External ISMS communications in the period (client security updates, incident notifications, certification body correspondence)
items.questions:
• Which ISMS topics must be communicated to staff, clients, suppliers or regulators?
• Who decides when an external party must be told something?
• Show me a recent example of a planned ISMS communication.
items.evidence: Communication plan; announcements and emails; meeting minutes; client communications; incident notification records

items.title: Inventory of information and other associated assets
items.guidance: Verify an inventory of information and other associated assets exists, assigns owners and is kept accurate. Test accuracy in both directions: trace a sample of inventory entries to real assets, and trace a sample of real assets (laptops, cloud accounts, SaaS applications, data stores) back to the inventory.
items.intent: The organization knows what information and technology assets it has, where they are and who owns them.
items.verify:
Design: The inventory defines which asset types are included (endpoints, servers, cloud resources, SaaS, data sets, code repositories) and the attributes required, including owner.
Implementation: The inventory is populated and owners are assigned.
Operating effectiveness: The inventory is accurate and current when reconciled with discovery tools and reality.
items.inspect:
• Reconcile a sample in both directions between discovery sources (RMM or MDM device list, EDR console, cloud console, SaaS admin) and the inventory
• Each sampled asset has a current owner
• Information assets (data sets, client data, repositories) are included, not only hardware
• Date of the last reconciliation
items.questions:
• How is the inventory updated when devices, cloud resources or SaaS apps are added?
• Where are information assets such as data sets and client data recorded?
• How often is the inventory reconciled with the RMM, MDM or cloud consoles?
items.evidence: Asset inventory; RMM or MDM device exports; EDR device list; cloud resource inventory; SaaS or application register; data inventory

items.title: Acceptable use of information and other associated assets
items.guidance: Verify rules for acceptable use and handling of information and assets are documented, communicated and acknowledged. Ask a few users how they would handle a specific case, such as client data on a personal device or use of an unapproved AI tool, and compare their answers with the rules.
items.intent: People know what they may and may not do with the organization's information and equipment, and those rules are applied.
items.verify:
Design: The acceptable use rules cover devices, email, internet, cloud and SaaS, generative AI tools, personal use and removable media.
Implementation: Staff and contractors have acknowledged the rules, and technical controls support key rules where practical.
Operating effectiveness: Violations are detected and handled, and the rules keep pace with new technology.
items.inspect:
• Currency of the Acceptable Use Policy (does it address current technology such as SaaS sharing and AI tools?)
• Acknowledgement records for a sample of personnel, including contractors
• Technical enforcement of key rules (web filtering, application control, DLP, MDM restrictions)
• Examples of acceptable use violations and how they were handled
items.questions:
• What is and is not allowed with company or client data in public AI tools?
• How are contractors made aware of acceptable use rules?
• How would a violation be detected?
items.evidence: Acceptable Use Policy; acknowledgement records; web filter, DLP and MDM policies; HR case summaries (aggregate only)

items.title: Return of assets
items.guidance: Sample recent leavers and role changes and verify company equipment, access tokens and information were returned or recovered, with a record of what was returned and when. Confirm how company information held on personally owned devices or accounts is recovered or removed.
items.intent: When people leave or their arrangements end, the organization recovers its equipment, information and access tokens.
items.verify:
Design: The offboarding process lists assets to return (devices, tokens, badges, data) and who collects them.
Implementation: Returns are recorded for each leaver.
Operating effectiveness: All assets are recovered; unrecovered devices are locked or wiped and escalated.
items.inspect:
• Sample three to five leavers from the HR list: return records and device status in the RMM or MDM (retired, wiped or reassigned)
• Handling of company data on personal devices at exit
• Unreturned assets and the actions taken
items.questions:
• How does IT learn that someone is leaving, and when?
• What happens if a device is not returned?
• How is company data removed from personal devices at exit?
items.evidence: HR leaver list; offboarding tickets and checklists; asset inventory status changes; MDM wipe or retire logs; return receipts

items.title: Classification of information
items.guidance: Verify a classification scheme exists that reflects confidentiality, integrity, availability and relevant interested party requirements, and that owners have classified their information. Sample several information types or repositories and confirm the classification is reasonable and known to users. The number and names of levels are the organization's choice.
items.intent: Information is sorted into sensitivity levels so protection matches its value and the expectations of clients, regulators and other interested parties.
items.verify:
Design: A classification scheme with defined levels and criteria exists and reflects legal and contractual requirements (e.g., client data and any regulated data).
Implementation: Information assets and repositories are classified, with owners responsible for the classification.
Operating effectiveness: Staff classify consistently, and classification drives handling (A.5.13, A.5.14, A.8.12).
items.inspect:
• Classification policy and level definitions
• Sample repositories (the controlled document repository sites, data stores, client project folders) and check the recorded classification
• Ask staff to classify a sample document and compare with the scheme
• How classification links to handling rules
items.questions:
• What classification would client-provided data receive, and why?
• Who decides the classification of a new repository or data set?
• How does classification change how information is stored or shared?
items.evidence: Data Classification Policy; data inventory; sensitivity label configuration (e.g., Microsoft Purview); repository metadata

items.title: Labelling of information
items.guidance: Verify labeling procedures are defined for the classification scheme and applied to information in its different forms. Sample documents, emails, repositories or system outputs and confirm labels appear where the procedure requires them. The procedure may exempt some information from labeling, so test against the organization's own rules.
items.intent: Information carries a visible or machine-readable marking of its classification, so people and systems handle it correctly.
items.verify:
Design: Labelling procedures cover electronic and physical formats and define exceptions (e.g., public information need not be labelled).
Implementation: Labelling mechanisms exist (sensitivity labels, headers and footers, metadata).
Operating effectiveness: Labels are applied consistently and are used by protective controls such as DLP or encryption.
items.inspect:
• Labelling procedure
• Sensitivity label configuration and usage reports, if used
• Sample documents and emails: does the label match the content?
• Whether labels trigger protections (encryption, sharing restrictions)
items.questions:
• How does someone label a confidential document?
• Are labels applied automatically, manually or both?
• What happens technically when something is labelled confidential?
items.evidence: Labelling procedure; sensitivity label policies and activity reports; document templates; DLP rules

items.title: Information transfer
items.guidance: Verify transfer rules, procedures or agreements cover each channel in use, such as email, file sharing, removable media and client or supplier data exchanges. Sample two or three recent transfers of sensitive or client information and confirm the approved method and protections, such as encryption or a secure portal, were used.
items.intent: Information moving within the organization or to other parties travels by approved, secure means under agreed rules.
items.verify:
Design: Transfer rules by classification and method (email, file sharing, secure transfer, removable media, verbal) exist, and agreements cover transfers with clients and suppliers.
Implementation: Approved transfer mechanisms are configured (encryption in transit, external sharing controls).
Operating effectiveness: Staff use approved methods, and unapproved methods are blocked or detected.
items.inspect:
• Information transfer rules and client or supplier data transfer terms
• External sharing settings in the collaboration platform (anonymous links, guest access)
• Email encryption and TLS configuration
• Sample recent transfers of client data: method used compared with the rule
items.questions:
• How would you send a large confidential data set to a client?
• Can staff create anonymous sharing links?
• What agreements govern how client data moves to and from the organization?
items.evidence: Information transfer rules; Microsoft 365 or the controlled document repository sharing settings; email encryption configuration; secure file transfer logs; contract data transfer terms

items.title: Access control
items.guidance: Verify access-control rules are defined based on business and security requirements and are applied consistently. Review applicable access policies, role/access models, provisioning practices, and samples of user access to confirm access is appropriately restricted.
items.intent: Access to information, systems and premises is granted according to clear rules based on business need and least privilege.
items.verify:
Design: Access control rules define principles such as least privilege, need-to-know, role-based access, approval requirements and review frequency.
Implementation: Access models (groups, roles) in key systems implement those rules.
Operating effectiveness: Actual access matches the rules, and deviations are caught by review.
items.inspect:
• Access control policy or principles
• Role and group design in the identity provider and in two or three key applications
• Sample users: does their access match their job?
• Results from A.5.16 to A.5.18 and A.8.2 to A.8.5 as supporting evidence
items.questions:
• How is access to a new system requested and approved?
• How do you decide what access a role needs?
• How are exceptions to the access rules approved?
items.evidence: Access Control Policy; identity provider groups and roles (e.g., Entra ID); application role matrices; access request tickets

items.title: Identity management
items.guidance: Verify identities are unique and managed through their full life cycle, and that shared, generic and service accounts are approved, owned and controlled. Reconcile a sample of accounts in the identity provider against HR records to find orphaned, duplicate or unowned identities.
items.intent: Every account, human or not, is created, changed and removed in a controlled way, so each identity is accountable and none linger unused.
items.verify:
Design: The identity life cycle process covers unique IDs, shared or generic accounts, service accounts and ownership.
Implementation: Accounts are created from authorized requests, and service and shared accounts are inventoried with owners.
Operating effectiveness: Leaver accounts are disabled promptly, and orphaned, shared and stale accounts are found and resolved.
items.inspect:
• Reconcile five leavers from HR against account disable dates in the identity provider and key SaaS applications
• Stale accounts inactive beyond a defined period (e.g., 90 days)
• Shared, generic and service accounts: inventory, owner and justification
• Guest and external accounts: sponsor and review
items.questions:
• How quickly are accounts disabled when someone leaves, and how is that checked?
• Which shared or service accounts exist, and who owns each?
• How are guest accounts reviewed and removed?
items.evidence: Identity provider user exports and sign-in activity; HR joiner and leaver reports; onboarding and offboarding tickets; service account inventory; guest account reports

items.title: Authentication information
items.guidance: Verify authentication information such as passwords, keys and secrets is issued and managed securely and that users know their responsibilities for protecting it. Check password and authentication settings in the identity provider, and confirm how secrets used by systems and code are stored, for example in a vault rather than in scripts or repositories.
items.intent: Passwords, keys, tokens and other secrets are issued, stored and handled so they are not guessed, shared or exposed.
items.verify:
Design: Rules cover initial credential issue, password construction, secure storage in a password manager or vault, secrets handling and resets after compromise.
Implementation: Temporary credentials are unique and must be changed at first use, and shared and privileged secrets are stored in a password manager or vault.
Operating effectiveness: Secrets are not kept in plain text (code, scripts, documents), and compromised credentials are reset promptly.
items.inspect:
• Password and authentication rules compared with identity provider configuration
• Password manager or vault use for shared and administrative credentials
• Secret scanning results in code repositories, if applicable
• Credential resets following suspected compromise
items.questions:
• How are initial passwords delivered to new users?
• Where are shared and service account credentials stored?
• What happens when a credential is suspected to be compromised?
• How do developers keep secrets out of source code?
items.evidence: Password rules; identity provider password and MFA settings; password manager admin console; secrets vault; repository secret scanning reports; help desk reset tickets

items.title: Secure authentication
items.guidance: Verify secure authentication is implemented in line with the access control policy, for example multi-factor authentication for remote, privileged and cloud access. Check identity provider and conditional access settings, and review any MFA exclusions or legacy authentication for approval and justification.
items.intent: Sign-in methods are strong enough for the access they protect, with multi-factor authentication where the risk calls for it.
items.verify:
Design: The authentication standard defines where MFA is required (all users, remote access, privileged access, cloud apps), acceptable methods, session controls and blocking of legacy protocols.
Implementation: MFA is enforced through the identity provider or conditional access, and legacy authentication is blocked.
Operating effectiveness: MFA coverage is complete with justified exclusions only, and risky sign-ins are monitored and acted on.
items.inspect:
• Conditional access and MFA policies, especially the exclusion list and its justification
• MFA registration report: users without MFA
• Legacy authentication blocked
• Key applications outside SSO and how MFA is enforced there
• Risky sign-in reports and the response
items.questions:
• Are any accounts excluded from MFA, and why?
• Which applications are not behind SSO, and how is MFA enforced for them?
• How are risky or impossible-travel sign-ins handled?
items.evidence: Conditional access policies; MFA registration reports; sign-in logs; SSO application list; identity protection reports

items.title: Access rights
items.guidance: Sample joiners, movers and leavers and verify access was requested, approved by the right owner, provisioned as approved, and removed or adjusted promptly. Review the most recent periodic access review for a key system and confirm findings were acted on.
items.intent: People have the access their current role requires and no more, and access is adjusted or removed promptly when needs change.
items.verify:
Design: Provisioning requires authorization, and periodic access reviews are defined (frequency, reviewers, systems).
Implementation: Access reviews are performed for key systems, and role changes trigger access changes.
