Operating effectiveness: Reviews lead to actual removals, and people who change roles do not accumulate access.
items.inspect:
• Sample five access grants: approval existed before provisioning
• Latest access review for two key systems: reviewer, date, decisions and evidence that removals were carried out
• Sample two internal role changes: previous access removed
items.questions:
• How often are access reviews performed, and by whom?
• What happened to the access flagged for removal in the last review?
• When someone changes roles, how is their old access removed?
items.evidence: Access request tickets; access review records and sign-offs; identity provider audit logs; application user lists

items.title: Privileged access rights
items.guidance: Verify privileged access is restricted, authorized, and reviewed at the interval the organization has set. Obtain the list of privileged accounts for key systems such as the identity provider, cloud consoles and production, confirm each is justified and approved, and check that admin tasks use separate accounts with strong authentication.
items.intent: Powerful administrative access is tightly limited, separately controlled and watched.
items.verify:
Design: Privileged access rules require separate admin accounts, least privilege, approval, just-in-time elevation where practical, MFA and periodic review.
Implementation: Privileged accounts are inventoried, separate from daily-use accounts and protected by MFA.
Operating effectiveness: Privileged access is reviewed, its use is monitored and leavers are removed.
items.inspect:
• Privileged accounts in the identity provider (e.g., Global Administrators), cloud consoles, servers, network devices and key SaaS apps
• Admins use separate accounts and MFA (phishing-resistant where feasible)
• Last privileged access review and the changes it produced
• Alerting on privileged role assignment or unusual admin activity
• Break-glass accounts: protection and monitoring
items.questions:
• How many people hold global or domain admin rights, and why?
• Do admins use a separate account for administration?
• How is privileged access requested, approved and removed?
• Who is alerted when someone is given admin rights?
items.evidence: Identity provider role assignment reports; privileged identity management or JIT configuration; privileged access review records; admin sign-in logs; break-glass procedure

items.title: Information access restriction
items.guidance: Verify access to information and application functions is restricted in line with the access control policy. Select a sensitive data set or client repository and confirm only authorized people and systems can reach it, testing effective permissions rather than relying on group names.
items.intent: People and systems can reach only the information and functions they are authorized to use.
items.verify:
Design: Repositories and applications have access models based on classification and need-to-know.
Implementation: Permissions are configured accordingly (e.g., client project sites limited to the project team).
Operating effectiveness: Permissions stay aligned over time: no broad access to sensitive data, and external sharing is controlled.
items.inspect:
• Sample three sensitive repositories (client data, HR, finance): membership compared with need-to-know
• Broad access groups (Everyone, All Users) on sensitive sites
• Permission and sharing reports
items.questions:
• Who can see client project data, and how is that limited to the project team?
• How are permissions removed when a project ends?
• How do you detect overly broad access?
items.evidence: the controlled document repository and OneDrive permission reports; data access governance reports; application role configuration; file share permissions

items.title: Operational planning and control
items.guidance: Verify the processes needed to meet ISMS requirements and deliver the risk treatment actions are planned, have operating criteria, and run as planned, including externally provided processes. Sample one or two outsourced or supplier-run processes and confirm how the organization controls them. Documented information is required to the extent needed for confidence that processes ran as planned; that extent is the organization's call.
items.intent: The processes that deliver the ISMS run in a controlled way: criteria are set, work follows them, records show it happened as planned, changes are managed, and outsourced processes that matter to the ISMS are kept under control.
items.verify:
Design: Criteria for ISMS operational processes are defined (procedures, standards, service levels).
Implementation: Processes operate to those criteria and produce records; externally provided processes (managed services, cloud, SaaS, contractors) are identified and controlled.
Operating effectiveness: Records give confidence that processes ran as planned, and unintended changes are reviewed with adverse effects mitigated.
items.inspect:
• List of externally provided processes relevant to the ISMS and how each is controlled (contract, service levels, reports, reviews)
• Records showing a sample of operational processes ran as planned
• An example of an unintended change and how its effects were reviewed
items.questions:
• Which ISMS-relevant processes are performed by external providers, and how are they controlled?
• How do you know operational security processes are carried out as planned?
• Describe a recent unplanned change and how its effects were handled.
items.evidence: Operating procedures; provider service levels and reports; supplier review records; ticketing records; change records

items.title: Information security in supplier relationships
items.guidance: Verify there is a defined approach for managing supplier security risk, including how suppliers are identified, assessed and tiered by the access or services they provide. Sample two or three critical suppliers and confirm a security risk assessment was done at onboarding and is current.
items.intent: The security risks that come with using suppliers are identified and managed through a defined process.
items.verify:
Design: The supplier security process defines risk tiering, due diligence requirements by tier and responsibilities.
Implementation: Suppliers are identified and tiered, and due diligence is done before higher-risk suppliers receive data or access.
Operating effectiveness: The process is applied to every new supplier, and the register is current.
items.inspect:
• Third-party register with risk tiers
• Sample two or three suppliers engaged in the period: due diligence (security questionnaire, SOC 2 report or ISO certificate review) completed before access or data was provided
• Suppliers with access to sensitive data or systems that are missing from the register
items.questions:
• How is a new supplier's security assessed before it receives data or access?
• Who decides a supplier's risk tier?
• How do you find suppliers engaged outside the process (e.g., SaaS bought on a corporate card)?
items.evidence: Third-Party Risk Management Policy; third-party register; due diligence records (questionnaires, SOC 2 reports, ISO certificates); procurement records; expense or SaaS discovery reports

items.title: Addressing information security within supplier agreements
items.guidance: Sample agreements with critical suppliers and verify they contain security requirements suited to the service, such as confidentiality, access, incident notification, subcontracting, assurance or audit rights, and return or deletion of data. Confirm requirements identified in the supplier risk assessment were carried into the contract.
items.intent: Security expectations are written into supplier agreements, in proportion to what each supplier does and can access.
items.verify:
Design: Standard security requirements are defined by supplier type (confidentiality, data protection, incident notification, right to audit, subcontracting, return or deletion of data).
Implementation: Agreements with key suppliers contain the relevant requirements.
Operating effectiveness: Requirements are enforceable and known to the supplier owner, and gaps are addressed at renewal or formally accepted.
items.inspect:
• Sample three higher-risk supplier contracts, DPAs or BAAs: incident notification, confidentiality, data handling, subprocessors, termination and data return
• For SaaS on click-through terms, evidence the terms were reviewed against requirements
• Contract gaps and how they were accepted or remediated
items.questions:
• Which security requirements must be in a contract with a supplier that processes client data?
• How are gaps handled when a supplier will not negotiate?
• How quickly must a key supplier notify you of a security incident?
items.evidence: Supplier contracts; DPAs and BAAs; security addenda; SaaS terms reviews; third-party register contract fields

items.title: Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
items.guidance: Verify risks in the ICT product and service supply chain are considered, such as a provider's own subcontractors, software components and hardware sources. Ask how security requirements flow down to sub-tier suppliers and how component provenance is assessed for critical systems. The depth of supply chain assurance should be proportionate to risk.
items.intent: Risks inherited through the technology supply chain, such as subprocessors, components and updates, are understood and managed.
items.verify:
Design: Requirements address supply chain risks such as subprocessors, software components, vendor updates and hardware sourcing.
Implementation: Key ICT suppliers' subprocessors and critical components are known, and software dependencies are tracked where the organization builds software.
Operating effectiveness: Supply chain events (a provider breach, a compromised update, a vulnerable dependency) are detected and acted on.
items.inspect:
• Subprocessor lists for key cloud and SaaS providers and how changes are notified
• Dependency scanning or SBOM practices where software is developed
• Response to a recent supply chain event (vendor breach notice, compromised package)
• Hardware purchased through authorized channels
items.questions:
• How would you learn that a key provider's subprocessor had been breached?
• How are third-party software libraries checked for known vulnerabilities?
• Describe your response to the most recent vendor security incident notice.
items.evidence: Subprocessor lists; dependency scanning or SBOM reports; vendor breach notices and response records; purchasing records

items.title: Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services
items.guidance: Verify supplier security performance is monitored and reviewed at defined intervals and when supplier services change. For critical suppliers, review evidence such as SOC 2 reports, certifications, review meetings or scorecards, and confirm exceptions and complementary user entity controls in those reports were evaluated.
items.intent: Suppliers' security and service performance are checked on an ongoing basis, and changes on their side are assessed before they create risk.
items.verify:
Design: Review frequency is set by supplier risk tier, and supplier changes trigger reassessment.
Implementation: Periodic reviews are performed (assurance report reviews, service level reviews, reassessments).
Operating effectiveness: Issues found in reviews are followed up, and supplier changes (new services, ownership, subprocessors) are reassessed.
items.inspect:
• Sample three high-risk suppliers: date of latest review compared with required frequency
• Evidence SOC reports were actually read (exceptions noted, complementary user entity controls considered)
• Service review meetings or service level reports for key providers (e.g., managed IT or security provider)
• Supplier changes in the period and whether reassessment occurred
items.questions:
• When was each critical supplier last reviewed?
• What did the latest SOC 2 report for [key supplier] say about exceptions, and what did you do?
• Which complementary user entity controls are you responsible for?
items.evidence: Third-party register review dates; annual supplier review records; SOC report review notes; service level reports and review minutes

items.title: Information security for use of cloud services
items.guidance: Verify processes exist for acquiring, using, managing and exiting cloud services, including a clear understanding of the shared responsibility split. Sample key cloud services and confirm the organization's side of that split is implemented, such as tenant security settings, access, logging and backup. Confirm exit and data retrieval arrangements were considered.
items.intent: Cloud services are chosen, configured, operated and eventually exited in a way that meets the organization's security requirements. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Cloud use requirements define approval, shared responsibility, configuration baselines and exit planning.
Implementation: Cloud services in use are known and approved, and the organization's side of the shared responsibility model is implemented.
Operating effectiveness: Cloud configuration is monitored and remediated, and exit or data return is planned for critical services.
items.inspect:
• Approved cloud services compared with discovered usage (SSO application list, CASB or expense data)
• Shared responsibility mapping for the primary platforms (e.g., Microsoft 365, Azure or AWS)
• Configuration posture reports (e.g., Microsoft Secure Score or a cloud posture tool) and remediation
• Exit or termination plans for critical cloud services
items.questions:
• How is a new cloud service approved?
• Which security responsibilities stay with you on your primary cloud platform?
• How are cloud misconfigurations detected?
• How would you retrieve your data if a cloud provider relationship ended?
items.evidence: Cloud services register; SSO application list; posture or Secure Score reports; shared responsibility documentation; cloud contracts and exit terms

items.title: Physical security perimeters
items.area: Premises, secure areas and physical monitoring
items.guidance: Verify security perimeters are defined for premises and areas holding information and associated assets, and that they are physically sound. Walk the office perimeter and check entry points, windows and shared areas; for cloud-hosted infrastructure, confirm data center perimeters are covered through supplier assurance (A.5.19 to A.5.23).
items.intent: Areas holding information and equipment have defined, physically sound boundaries.
items.verify:
Design: Perimeters are defined for offices, network or server rooms and storage areas.
Implementation: Perimeters are physically sound (walls, doors, windows, locks) and responsibilities with the landlord are clear.
Operating effectiveness: Perimeter controls remain intact, and weak entry points are addressed.
items.inspect:
• Site walkthrough: doors, windows, emergency exits and shared-building boundaries
• Floor plan showing any defined secure areas
• Landlord or building security arrangements
• For cloud-hosted systems, provider SOC 2 or ISO reports covering physical security
items.questions:
• Which areas contain sensitive information or equipment?
• What is the organization responsible for, and what does the landlord handle?
• Where are servers and network equipment located?
items.evidence: Floor plans; site security assessment; lease or building security terms; cloud provider SOC 2 or ISO reports
items.guidance_notes: Where infrastructure is cloud hosted, physical controls at the provider's facilities are assured through supplier assurance (A.5.19 to A.5.23), not by site inspection. Confirm the SoA reflects which premises are in scope.

items.title: Physical entry
items.area: Premises, secure areas and physical monitoring
items.guidance: Verify entry to secure areas is protected by appropriate entry controls such as badges, keys or reception. Compare the badge or key issuance list with current staff, check visitor logs for a sample of dates, and confirm leavers' physical access was removed.
items.intent: Only authorized people get into secure areas, and entry is controlled and recorded.
items.verify:
Design: Entry rules cover badges or keys, visitors and deliveries.
Implementation: Access systems are configured and visitor records are kept.
Operating effectiveness: Badge access is reviewed, leavers' badges are disabled and visitors are escorted.
items.inspect:
• Badge system user list compared with current staff (sample leavers)
• Sample of the visitor log
• Key register
• Observe visitor handling and tailgating during the walkthrough
items.questions:
• How are badges issued and deactivated?
• How are visitors handled?
• Who reviews physical access rights, and how often?
items.evidence: Badge system access reports; visitor logs; key register; physical access review records

items.title: Securing offices, rooms and facilities
items.area: Premises, secure areas and physical monitoring
items.guidance: Verify physical security is designed and applied to offices, rooms and facilities that need it, such as locked comms or server rooms and restricted areas holding sensitive information. Walk through the office and confirm the rooms identified as needing protection are secured in practice.
items.intent: Offices, rooms and facilities are physically protected in proportion to what they contain.
items.verify:
Design: Sensitive rooms (network closet, records storage) are identified with suitable protection, and signage does not reveal sensitive activities unnecessarily.
Implementation: Locks and restricted access are in place.
Operating effectiveness: Rooms are found secured during observation.
items.inspect:
• Walkthrough of network or server closets, storage rooms and meeting rooms
• Who holds keys or access to those rooms
items.questions:
• Who can access the network closet?
• How is confidential material stored in the office?
items.evidence: Walkthrough observations; access lists; key register

items.title: Physical security monitoring
items.area: Premises, secure areas and physical monitoring
items.guidance: Verify premises are monitored for unauthorized physical access by the means the organization has chosen, such as alarms, CCTV, building management or guard services. Check monitoring is operating, alerts reach someone who responds, and recordings are retained and protected. In shared or leased buildings, confirm what the landlord provides and what the organization relies on.
items.intent: Unauthorized physical access to the premises would be detected. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: The monitoring approach (CCTV, intrusion alarm, access logs, guarding) is proportionate to risk.
Implementation: Monitoring systems are installed and working, with retention defined.
Operating effectiveness: Alerts are responded to, footage and logs are reviewed when needed, and systems are tested and maintained.
items.inspect:
• CCTV coverage of entry points and recording retention
• Alarm monitoring arrangement and test records
• Access log review practice
• Any physical security events and how they were handled
items.questions:
• Who is alerted if there is an after-hours entry?
• How long is footage kept?
• When was the alarm last tested?
items.evidence: CCTV and alarm configuration; monitoring contracts; alarm test records; badge access logs

items.title: Protecting against physical and environmental threats
items.area: Premises, secure areas and physical monitoring
items.guidance: Verify protection against physical and environmental threats, such as fire, flood, power disruption and severe weather, has been assessed and implemented for premises and equipment. Check fire detection and suppression and equipment placement relative to water or heat, and link to the Clause 4.1 climate change determination where relevant.
items.intent: Premises and equipment are protected against fire, flood, storms and other physical and environmental hazards relevant to the site.
items.verify:
Design: Environmental threats are identified for each site (e.g., regional severe weather, flooding, fire).
Implementation: Protections are in place (fire detection and suppression, water detection, equipment raised off the floor, reliance on resilient cloud hosting).
Operating effectiveness: Protections are inspected and maintained, and severe weather preparations are exercised.
items.inspect:
• Site threat assessment
• Fire system inspection records
• Environmental sensors and alerts
• Severe weather preparedness procedure and equipment placement
items.questions:
• Which environmental threats matter most for each site?
• What happens to on-site equipment ahead of a severe weather event?
• When were the fire systems last inspected?
items.evidence: Site threat assessment; fire inspection records; environmental sensor alerts; severe weather and continuity procedures
items.guidance_notes: This control may connect to the climate change determination in Clause 4.1 (Amd 1:2024).

items.title: Working in secure areas
items.area: Premises, secure areas and physical monitoring
items.guidance: Verify security measures for working in secure areas are defined and followed, such as limits on unsupervised work and on photography or recording devices. If no secure areas exist on premises, confirm the SoA justification reflects this.
items.intent: Work inside secure areas follows rules that keep those areas secure.
items.verify:
Design: Rules for secure areas are defined (no unsupervised third parties, restrictions on photography or recording).
Implementation: Rules are communicated or posted.
Operating effectiveness: Rules are followed, and third-party work in secure areas is supervised.
items.inspect:
• Secure area rules
• Observation during the walkthrough
• Vendor or contractor access records for secure areas
items.questions:
• Who may work in the server or network room unsupervised?
• How are vendor technicians supervised?
items.evidence: Secure area rules; visitor and contractor logs; walkthrough observations
items.guidance_notes: If no secure areas exist on premises, confirm the SoA exclusion or justification.

items.title: Clear desk and clear screen
items.area: Premises, secure areas and physical monitoring
items.guidance: Verify clear desk and clear screen rules are defined, communicated and followed. Walk through workspaces unannounced, after hours if practical, looking for unattended sensitive papers, unlocked screens and removable media, and confirm automatic screen lock is enforced technically.
items.intent: Information is not left exposed on unattended desks, printers or screens.
items.verify:
Design: A clear desk and clear screen policy exists and covers home working.
Implementation: Screen lock is enforced by configuration, lockable storage is available and printing is controlled.
Operating effectiveness: Observation confirms compliance, and periodic checks are performed.
items.inspect:
• Screen lock timeout settings in MDM or group policy
• Walkthrough (with permission) for unattended papers and unlocked screens
• Printer pickup practice and secure print, if used
• Guidance for remote workers
items.questions:
• How long before an unattended screen locks, and is that enforced technically?
• How are printed confidential documents handled?
• Are clear desk checks performed, and by whom?
items.evidence: Clear Desk and Clear Screen Policy; MDM or group policy screen lock settings; walkthrough notes; spot-check records

items.title: Equipment siting and protection
items.guidance: Verify equipment is sited and protected to reduce environmental risks and unauthorized access, for example network equipment in locked cabinets and screens positioned away from public view. Inspect a sample of equipment locations in the office.
items.intent: Equipment is placed and protected so it is not easily damaged, tampered with or overlooked.
items.verify:
Design: Siting requirements cover environmental hazards, viewing by unauthorized people and tampering.
Implementation: Equipment is placed accordingly.
Operating effectiveness: Protection is maintained over time.
items.inspect:
• Walkthrough of network equipment, printers and displays visible from windows or public areas
• Condition of the network closet (temperature, cleanliness, UPS)
items.questions:
• How is network equipment protected from tampering or damage?
• Are any screens showing sensitive information visible to visitors?
items.evidence: Walkthrough observations; network closet photos; environmental monitoring

items.title: Supporting utilities
items.guidance: Verify information processing facilities are protected against failures of supporting utilities such as power, telecommunications and HVAC. Check UPS or generator provision and testing for on-premises equipment; for cloud-hosted services, confirm utility resilience is covered through supplier assurance.
items.intent: Power, connectivity and other supporting utilities do not become a single point of failure for on-site equipment.
items.verify:
Design: Utility dependencies (power, internet, cooling) are identified, with resilience proportionate to the importance of on-site equipment.
Implementation: UPS, generator or redundant internet are in place where needed.
Operating effectiveness: UPS and generator are tested and maintained, and alerts are monitored.
items.inspect:
• UPS status and battery test records
• Generator test records, if applicable
• Internet service redundancy
• Cooling for the network closet
items.questions:
• What happens to on-site equipment during a power outage?
• When were UPS batteries last tested?
• Is there a secondary internet connection?
items.evidence: UPS management console; maintenance records; ISP contracts; generator test logs

items.title: Cabling security
items.guidance: Verify power, data and supporting cables are protected from interception, interference or damage. Inspect comms rooms and cable routes in the office for exposed or unsecured cabling and labeling; in leased premises, confirm which cabling is under the organization's control.
items.intent: Power and data cabling is protected from damage, interference and interception.
items.verify:
Design: Cabling standards cover enclosure, labelling and protection of network ports in public areas.
Implementation: Cabling is installed accordingly.
Operating effectiveness: Unused network ports are disabled or controlled, and patch panels are secured.
items.inspect:
• Walkthrough of patch panels and exposed cabling
• Network ports in public or meeting areas
• Switch port security or network access control configuration
items.questions:
• Could a visitor plug into a meeting room network port and reach internal systems?
• Where are the patch panels, and who can access them?
items.evidence: Walkthrough observations; switch port configuration; network access control settings; cabling documentation

items.title: Equipment maintenance
items.guidance: Verify equipment is maintained to manufacturer recommendations or defined schedules so it stays available and secure. Sample maintenance records for key equipment such as UPS, network devices and fire systems, and confirm third-party maintenance is supervised and data is protected when equipment leaves site.
items.intent: Equipment is maintained so it stays available and does not put information at risk during servicing.
items.verify:
Design: Maintenance requirements follow manufacturer recommendations and use authorized personnel or service contracts.
Implementation: Maintenance is performed and recorded, third-party maintenance is supervised, and data is protected when equipment leaves for repair.
Operating effectiveness: Maintenance records are current and failures are addressed.
items.inspect:
• Service records for network equipment, UPS and cooling
• Support and warranty contracts
• Process for sending devices for repair, including data removal
items.questions:
• Who maintains network and power equipment?
• How is data protected when a laptop goes out for repair?
items.evidence: Service contracts; maintenance logs; repair or RMA tickets; warranty status reports

items.title: Storage media
items.guidance: Verify storage media are managed through acquisition, use, transport and disposal in line with the classification scheme and handling rules. Check whether removable media use is technically restricted, how exceptions are authorized, and sample disposal records.
items.intent: Removable and other storage media are controlled from purchase to disposal, in line with the sensitivity of what they hold.
items.verify:
Design: Rules cover removable media use, encryption, transport and disposal.
Implementation: Technical controls (USB blocking or enforced encryption) are configured, and any media in use is inventoried.
Operating effectiveness: Media use matches the rules, and disposal is evidenced.
items.inspect:
• Removable media control policies in endpoint management or EDR
• Approved exceptions
• Media destruction certificates
• Handling of any physical backup media
items.questions:
• Can staff use USB drives? If so, how are they protected?
• How is old media destroyed?
items.evidence: Device control policies; exception approvals; destruction certificates; media inventory

items.title: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment
items.guidance: Verify equipment containing storage media is checked so sensitive data and licensed software are removed or securely overwritten before disposal or re-use. Sample recent disposals or re-issued laptops and confirm wipe or destruction records, including certificates from disposal vendors.
items.intent: Equipment is wiped or destroyed so that no sensitive data or licensed software leaves with it on disposal or re-use.
items.verify:
Design: The disposal and re-use procedure defines sanitization methods (e.g., in line with NIST SP 800-88), verification and certificates.
Implementation: A disposal provider issues certificates, and devices are wiped before re-issue.
Operating effectiveness: Sampled disposed or re-issued devices have wipe or destruction evidence matched by serial number.
items.inspect:
• Sample three to five retired devices from the inventory and match serial numbers to destruction certificates or wipe logs
• Wipe evidence for devices re-issued to another user
• Disposal provider agreement
items.questions:
• What happens to a laptop before it is re-issued to another employee?
• How do you confirm the disposal provider destroyed the drives?
• Can serial numbers be matched to certificates?
items.evidence: Destruction certificates; asset inventory disposal records; wipe or reset logs (MDM, Autopilot); disposal provider contract

items.title: User endpoint devices
items.guidance: Verify information on or accessible through user endpoint devices is protected, including encryption, device management, patching, screen lock and remote wipe. Review device management compliance reports and sample several devices, including any personally owned devices allowed to access company data.
items.intent: Information on laptops, desktops and mobile devices is protected by consistent device security, whoever uses the device and wherever it is.
items.verify:
Design: An endpoint baseline defines encryption, EDR, patching, screen lock, local admin restriction, MDM enrollment and rules for personal devices.
Implementation: Devices are enrolled and configured to the baseline.
Operating effectiveness: Compliance reports show devices meet the baseline, and noncompliant devices are blocked or remediated.
items.inspect:
• Endpoint security baseline or standard
• MDM or RMM compliance report: sample five devices for encryption, healthy EDR agent, supported and patched OS, and local admin status
• Reconcile device counts across the inventory, MDM and EDR to find unmanaged devices
• Conditional access that blocks noncompliant devices
items.questions:
• How do you know every laptop has encryption and EDR running?
• What happens to a device that falls out of compliance?
• Can personal devices access company email or files, and under what controls?
items.evidence: MDM or RMM compliance dashboards (e.g., Intune, NinjaOne); EDR console; conditional access policies; asset inventory

items.title: Remote working
items.guidance: Verify remote working rules are defined and communicated, covering areas such as device use, network connections, physical privacy and handling of printed or client information. Interview a few remote workers and check technical enforcement, such as VPN or conditional access, device compliance and screen lock settings.
items.intent: Information stays protected when people work away from the office.
items.verify:
Design: Remote working rules define requirements (managed devices, secure remote access, MFA, home network, screen privacy, printing).
Implementation: Technical controls enforce the key requirements (device compliance, conditional access, disk encryption, EDR).
Operating effectiveness: Remote devices are compliant, exceptions are tracked and staff know the rules.
items.inspect:
• Remote working policy
• Conditional access and device compliance policies (e.g., requiring a compliant device or MFA for remote access)
• Device compliance report: sample remote users' devices for encryption, healthy EDR and current patches
• Rules for personal devices if they are allowed
items.questions:
• What prevents someone accessing company data from an unmanaged personal device?
• How is the security of remote workers' devices checked?
• What are the rules for working in public places?
items.evidence: Remote Working Policy; conditional access policies; MDM compliance reports; EDR device list; VPN or zero-trust access configuration

items.title: Security of assets off-premises
items.guidance: Verify assets used off-site, such as laptops and mobile devices, are protected through measures such as encryption, remote wipe and rules for travel and public spaces. Check device management reports for encryption and compliance status on a sample of devices.
items.intent: Laptops, phones and other assets stay protected when used away from the organization's premises.
items.verify:
Design: Rules cover laptops and mobile devices off site (encryption, not leaving devices unattended, travel guidance) and equipment in home offices.
Implementation: Encryption and remote lock or wipe are enabled, and asset records show who holds each device.
Operating effectiveness: Lost or stolen devices are reported, locked or wiped, and recorded.
items.inspect:
• MDM encryption compliance report
• Remote lock or wipe capability
• Lost or stolen device tickets and actions taken
• Travel guidance
items.questions:
• What happens when a laptop is lost?
• Can you show that every laptop is encrypted?
• Are there rules for international travel?
items.evidence: MDM and encryption compliance reports (e.g., BitLocker, FileVault); lost device tickets; asset assignment records

items.title: Protection against malware
items.guidance: Verify malware protection is implemented and supported by user awareness, such as endpoint protection on all devices and email filtering. Reconcile the endpoint protection console with the device inventory to find unprotected devices, and review how detections are handled.
items.intent: Systems are protected against malware, backed by staff who know how to avoid and report it.
items.verify:
Design: The anti-malware standard defines coverage, configuration, updates and response.
Implementation: EDR or anti-malware is deployed on all endpoints and servers, with email filtering and tamper protection.
Operating effectiveness: Coverage is complete, agents are healthy and current, and detections are responded to.
items.inspect:
• EDR device count compared with the asset inventory to find unprotected devices
• Policy settings: protect versus detect mode, tamper protection, and exclusions with their justification
• Sample three recent detections: response and closure
• Email security filtering configuration
items.questions:
• How do you know every endpoint and server has a healthy EDR agent?
• Who responds to malware detections, including after hours?
• What exclusions are configured in the EDR policy, and why?
items.evidence: EDR or MDR console (e.g., SentinelOne, Huntress, Microsoft Defender); detection and response tickets; email security reports; exclusion list

items.title: Use of privileged utility programs
items.guidance: Verify use of utility programs that can override system or application controls is restricted and tightly controlled. Identify such tools in the environment, such as admin, remote management or scripting tools, confirm who can use them, and check that use is logged.
items.intent: Tools that can bypass normal system and application controls are limited to those who need them, and their use is controlled.
items.verify:
Design: Privileged utilities are identified (remote administration tools, RMM scripting, PowerShell, password recovery tools) with rules for their use.
Implementation: Access is limited to authorized administrators, and application control limits what standard users can run.
Operating effectiveness: Use is logged and reviewed, and unauthorized tools are detected.
items.inspect:
• List of authorized administration and remote access tools
• Who can run scripts through the RMM
• Application control or EDR policies that block unauthorized utilities
• RMM script execution logs
items.questions:
• Which tools can bypass normal controls, such as an RMM remote shell?
• Who can use them, and is use logged?
• How would an unauthorized remote access tool be detected?
items.evidence: RMM role permissions and activity logs; application control policies; EDR detections for remote access tools

items.title: Configuration management
items.guidance: Verify security configurations and baselines for hardware, software, services and networks are defined, implemented, monitored and reviewed. Compare a sample of systems with the defined baselines, such as CIS Benchmarks or Intune policies, and check how configuration drift is detected and corrected.
items.intent: Systems are built and kept to defined secure configurations, and drift from them is detected and corrected. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Secure baselines are defined for endpoints, servers, cloud tenants and network devices (e.g., based on CIS Benchmarks).
Implementation: Baselines are applied through automation (MDM profiles, group policy, infrastructure as code).
Operating effectiveness: Drift is detected and corrected, baselines are reviewed, and configuration changes go through change management.
items.inspect:
• Baseline documents for each platform
• MDM, group policy or infrastructure-as-code settings compared with the baseline
• Drift or compliance reports (e.g., Secure Score, CIS benchmark scans)
• Configuration backups for network devices
items.questions:
• Which baseline is used for each platform?
• How is configuration drift detected?
• Who approves changes to a baseline?
items.evidence: Configuration baselines; MDM configuration profiles; cloud posture reports; infrastructure-as-code repositories; network configuration backups

items.title: Installation of software on operational systems
items.guidance: Verify software installation on operational systems is securely managed. Check whether users can install software, how installation requests are approved, and compare installed software on a sample of systems with the approved list.
items.intent: Software on operational systems is installed only through controlled, approved means.
items.verify:
Design: Rules define who can install software, what is approved and how approval is requested.
Implementation: Standard users lack local admin rights, and software is deployed through management tools or controlled by application control.
Operating effectiveness: Unauthorized software is detected and removed.
items.inspect:
• Local admin rights report
• Approved software list
• RMM software inventory compared with the approved list (look for unusual titles)
• Software request tickets
items.questions:
• Can a standard user install software?
• How is new software requested and approved?
• How is unauthorized software detected?
items.evidence: RMM software inventory; local admin reports; approved software catalog; software request tickets; application control policies

items.title: Management of technical vulnerabilities
items.guidance: Verify vulnerability information is obtained, exposure is evaluated, and appropriate action is taken. Review recent scan results and patch reports, sample several critical findings, and confirm they were fixed within the organization's target timeframes or have an approved exception.
items.intent: Known technical weaknesses are found, assessed and fixed or mitigated promptly according to risk.
items.verify:
Design: The vulnerability management process defines scan scope and frequency, remediation timeframes by severity and an exception process.
Implementation: Scanning covers endpoints, servers, cloud, external perimeter and applications, and patches are deployed.
Operating effectiveness: Remediation meets the timeframes, exceptions have risk acceptance, and actively exploited vulnerabilities are prioritized.
items.inspect:
• Remediation timeframes by severity
• Most recent scan results, trend and scan coverage compared with the inventory
• Patch compliance for operating systems and third-party applications
• Sample three critical or high vulnerabilities: time to remediate against the timeframe
• Penetration test results and remediation status
• Exceptions and risk acceptances
items.questions:
• What is the required timeframe to fix a critical vulnerability, and is it being met?
• How are vulnerabilities in third-party applications and cloud services identified?
• Which vulnerabilities are past due, and why?
• When was the last penetration test, and what remains open?
items.evidence: Vulnerability scanner reports; RMM patch reports; penetration test reports; remediation tickets; exception register

items.title: Networks security
items.guidance: Verify networks and network devices are secured, managed and controlled. Review network diagrams, device configuration management, administrative access to network devices, and a sample of firewall rules for business justification.
items.intent: Networks and network devices are secured and managed so they protect the systems and information connected to them.
items.verify:
Design: Network security architecture and device management rules cover firewalls, administrative access, firmware updates and remote access.
Implementation: Firewalls and network devices are configured to the rules, management interfaces are restricted and remote access requires MFA.
Operating effectiveness: Firewall rules are reviewed, firmware is current and configurations are backed up.
items.inspect:
• Network diagram
• Firewall rule review records
• Firmware versions compared with vendor-supported versions
• Administrative access to network devices
• Remote access configuration
items.questions:
• When were firewall rules last reviewed, and what was removed?
• How are network devices patched?
• Who can administer network devices?
items.evidence: Network diagrams; firewall configurations and rule reviews; firmware reports; VPN or remote access configuration

items.title: Security of network services
items.guidance: Verify security features, service levels and requirements for network services are identified, implemented and monitored, whether provided in-house or externally. Review agreements with internet, SD-WAN or cloud networking providers and confirm the required security features are configured.
items.intent: Network services, whether in-house or provided by others, deliver the security features and service levels the organization needs.
items.verify:
Design: Requirements for network services (internet provider, SD-WAN, DNS, managed firewall, cloud networking) are defined, including security features and service levels.
Implementation: Agreements include those requirements, and security features are enabled (e.g., DNS filtering, DDoS protection).
Operating effectiveness: Service performance and security are monitored.
items.inspect:
• Network service contracts and service levels
• Security features enabled
• Provider reports
items.questions:
• Which network services are provided by third parties?
• What security features do they provide, and how do you confirm they are working?
items.evidence: Internet or managed network contracts; service level reports; DNS filtering configuration

items.title: Segregation of networks
items.guidance: Verify groups of services, users and systems are separated on the network according to risk, for example guest, corporate, production and development networks. Review the segmentation design and check a sample of rules to confirm the separation is enforced.
items.intent: Networks are divided so that a problem in one group of users or systems does not spread freely to others.
items.verify:
Design: The segmentation design separates guest, corporate, server, management, IoT and development, test and production networks, including cloud virtual networks.
Implementation: Segmentation is implemented (VLANs, firewall rules, security groups).
Operating effectiveness: Segmentation works in practice (e.g., guest Wi-Fi cannot reach corporate systems).
items.inspect:
• Network diagram with segments
• VLAN and firewall configuration
• An authorized test from the guest network
• Cloud network security group rules
items.questions:
• How is guest Wi-Fi separated from corporate systems?
• How are production environments separated from development?
• When was segmentation last tested?
items.evidence: Network diagrams; VLAN and firewall configurations; cloud security group rules; penetration test results

items.title: Web filtering
items.guidance: Verify access to external websites is managed to reduce exposure to malicious content, for example through DNS filtering, a secure web gateway or endpoint web protection. Check the blocked categories, that filtering covers remote as well as office users, and how exceptions are approved.
items.intent: Access to harmful or unwanted websites is filtered to reduce exposure to malicious content. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Web filtering rules define blocked categories (malicious, phishing, newly registered domains) and an exception process.
Implementation: Filtering applies both on and off the corporate network (DNS or agent-based for remote users).
Operating effectiveness: Filtering covers all devices, exceptions are approved and logs are reviewed.
items.inspect:
• Web filter policy and blocked categories
• Coverage of remote devices
• Sample blocked events
• Exception requests
items.questions:
• Does web filtering protect laptops away from the corporate network?
• How are exceptions requested and approved?
• Which categories are blocked?
items.evidence: DNS or web filter console; agent deployment report; block logs; exception tickets

items.title: Use of cryptography
items.guidance: Verify rules for the use of cryptography, including key management, are defined and implemented. Check encryption in transit and at rest for key systems, such as TLS configuration and storage encryption, and confirm how keys and certificates are generated, stored, rotated and revoked.
items.intent: Encryption is used where it is needed, with sound choices of method and well-managed keys.
items.verify:
Design: The cryptography standard defines where encryption is required (at rest, in transit), approved algorithms and protocols, and key management responsibilities.
Implementation: Encryption is in place (disk, TLS, databases, backups), and keys and certificates are managed.
Operating effectiveness: Certificates are renewed before expiry, weak protocols are disabled and access to keys is restricted.
items.inspect:
• Cryptography policy
• Disk encryption compliance
• TLS configuration of public services (protocol versions)
• Certificate inventory and expiry tracking
• Access to key vaults
items.questions:
• Where is encryption required, and how do you verify it is applied?
• Who manages encryption keys and certificates?
• How are certificate expirations tracked?
items.evidence: Cryptography policy; encryption compliance reports; certificate inventory; key vault access logs; TLS scan results

items.title: Data leakage prevention
items.guidance: Verify data leakage prevention measures are applied to systems, networks and devices that handle sensitive information. Review DLP policies or equivalent controls for email, cloud sharing and endpoints, and confirm alerts are reviewed and acted on. The choice of technical measures is risk-based; agree any live test with the owner first.
items.intent: Sensitive information is kept from leaving through channels where it should not go, and attempts are detected. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Leakage channels are identified (email, cloud sharing, USB, uploads to AI tools, printing) and controls selected by classification.
Implementation: DLP policies (email, endpoint, cloud), sharing restrictions and device controls are configured.
Operating effectiveness: DLP alerts are reviewed and acted on, and policies are tuned.
items.inspect:
• DLP policy configuration and scope
• Alert reports and a sample of how alerts were handled
• External sharing reports
• Controls on uploads to unsanctioned cloud storage or AI tools
items.questions:
• Which data leakage channels concern you most?
• Who reviews DLP alerts?
• What would stop someone uploading client data to a personal cloud account?
items.evidence: DLP policies (e.g., Microsoft Purview); DLP alert reports; sharing audit logs; CASB or web filter reports

items.title: Data masking
items.guidance: Where sensitive data such as PII or client data is used outside production, for example in testing, analytics or model development, verify masking, pseudonymization or anonymization is applied as the organization's policies require. Ask how the organization decides when masking is needed and sample one data set used outside production.
items.intent: Sensitive data is masked, pseudonymized or de-identified where full values are not needed, in line with policy, business need and law. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Criteria define when masking, pseudonymization or de-identification is required (e.g., production or client data used for development, testing, analytics, support or model training).
Implementation: Masking techniques are implemented where required.
Operating effectiveness: Unmasked sensitive data is not used outside production without approval.
items.inspect:
• Masking or de-identification standards
• Sample non-production data sets or test environments for real sensitive data
• Approvals for any use of unmasked data
• Client contract requirements for de-identification
items.questions:
• When must data be masked or de-identified before use?
• How is test or analytics data prepared?
• Who can approve use of real client data outside production?
items.evidence: Data handling standards; masking or de-identification scripts and tools; test data approvals; client contracts
items.guidance_notes: Confirm applicability against the SoA; relevance depends on whether sensitive data is used outside production.

items.title: Information deletion
items.guidance: Verify information is deleted when no longer required, in line with retention rules and client or legal requirements. Sample a data set past its retention period or a recent client offboarding, and confirm deletion was performed and recorded, including copies held by suppliers where applicable.
items.intent: Information is deleted when it is no longer needed, including at suppliers and at the end of client engagements. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Deletion requirements are tied to the retention schedule, client contracts (return or deletion at the end of an engagement) and legal holds.
Implementation: Automated retention and deletion are configured, and client data deletion procedures exist.
Operating effectiveness: Deletion happens and is evidenced, including by suppliers.
items.inspect:
• Sample one or two ended client engagements: evidence data was returned or deleted as the contract requires
• Retention and deletion policy configuration
• Supplier deletion confirmations
• How deletion requests are handled for backups
items.questions:
• What happens to client data when an engagement ends?
• How is deletion confirmed and recorded?
• How are deletions handled in backups?
items.evidence: Retention schedule; deletion certificates or logs; Microsoft 365 retention policies; client offboarding checklists; supplier deletion confirmations

items.title: Information security in project management
items.guidance: Verify information security is built into project management so that security requirements and risks are identified early and reviewed at defined project stages, whatever the project type. Sample one or two recent projects, such as a new client engagement, platform change or model deployment, and confirm security was considered from initiation to closure.
items.intent: Projects deal with security risks from the start and throughout, rather than discovering them at go-live.
items.verify:
Design: The project methodology includes security steps (risk assessment, security requirements, sign-off) that apply regardless of project type.
Implementation: Recent projects show security requirements identified early and tracked.
Operating effectiveness: Security issues were resolved before go-live or formally accepted by the right person.
items.inspect:
• Project methodology or templates with security checkpoints
• Sample two recent projects (internal or client delivery): security risk assessment, requirements and go-live sign-off
• Security issues raised during projects and how they were resolved or accepted
items.questions:
• At what point in a project is security considered?
• Who signs off on security before go-live?
• Show me a recent project where security changed the design or the timeline.
items.evidence: Project charters and plans; project risk registers; security requirements; go-live checklists; project management tool records

items.title: Application security requirements
items.guidance: Verify security requirements are identified, specified and approved when applications are developed or acquired. Sample a recent development or acquisition and confirm requirements such as authentication, data protection and logging were documented and approved at the start.
items.intent: Security needs are defined and agreed before an application is built or bought, and checked before it goes live.
items.verify:
Design: A process defines security requirements (authentication, data protection, logging, input validation) for new applications and acquisitions.
Implementation: Requirements are documented for sampled developments and acquisitions.
Operating effectiveness: Requirements are verified during testing or acceptance.
items.inspect:
• Requirements documents or user stories with security acceptance criteria
• Security evaluation of recently acquired SaaS applications
• Client-specified security requirements for delivered applications
items.questions:
• How are security requirements defined for a new application or a client deliverable?
• How do you confirm purchased applications meet security requirements?
items.evidence: Requirements documents; user stories and acceptance criteria; vendor security evaluations
items.guidance_notes: Applies where the organization develops or maintains software, models or code. Confirm applicability and any exclusion justification against the SoA.

items.title: Secure system architecture and engineering principles
items.guidance: Verify secure engineering principles, such as defense in depth, least privilege and secure defaults, are documented, maintained and applied. Ask for the documented principles and confirm they were applied in a recent architecture decision or design review.
items.intent: Systems are designed and engineered according to agreed security principles.
items.verify:
Design: Documented principles exist (defense in depth, least privilege, zero trust, secure defaults, fail secure).
Implementation: Principles are applied in architecture and design reviews.
Operating effectiveness: Principles are reviewed and updated, and new systems are designed against them.
items.inspect:
• Architecture principles document
• Design review record for a recent system
• Exceptions to the principles and who approved them
items.questions:
• What security principles guide system design here?
• Show a recent design review.
• Who reviews architecture for security?
items.evidence: Architecture standards; design documents; architecture review records

items.title: Secure development life cycle
items.guidance: Verify rules for secure development are established and applied across the development life cycle, including models and data pipelines where applicable. Sample one or two recent releases and trace security activities through design, coding, testing and deployment.
items.intent: Software and systems are developed under a life cycle that builds security in at each stage.
items.verify:
Design: The SDLC defines security activities (requirements, design review, secure coding, code review, testing, release approval) and the environments used.
Implementation: The SDLC was applied to sampled projects or releases.
Operating effectiveness: Security activities are performed consistently, and security defects are fixed before release or formally accepted.
items.inspect:
• SDLC documentation
• Sample two recent releases: security requirements, code review, testing and approval
• Developer secure development training
items.questions:
• What security steps are required before code reaches production?
• Show me a recent release and its security checks.
• How are security defects prioritized?
items.evidence: SDLC policy; pull requests; CI/CD pipeline configuration; release records; SAST and DAST reports
items.guidance_notes: Applies where the organization develops or maintains software, models or code. Confirm applicability and any exclusion justification against the SoA.

items.title: Secure coding
items.guidance: Verify secure coding principles are applied in software development. Check for coding standards, static analysis or dependency scanning in the pipeline, peer review before merge, and how findings from these tools are resolved.
items.intent: Code is written in ways that avoid common security flaws. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Secure coding standards exist (e.g., based on OWASP guidance), covering approved libraries and secrets handling.
Implementation: Tools such as linters, SAST, dependency scanning and secret scanning are built into the development workflow.
Operating effectiveness: Findings are remediated, and code review checks for security issues.
items.inspect:
• Secure coding standard
• SAST and dependency scan results and their remediation
• Sample pull requests for security-focused review
• Secret scanning results
items.questions:
• What secure coding standard do developers follow?
• What happens when a scan finds a high-severity issue?
• Do code reviews check for security issues?
items.evidence: Coding standards; SAST and SCA reports; pull request reviews; secret scanning alerts
items.guidance_notes: Applies where the organization develops or maintains software, models or code. Confirm applicability and any exclusion justification against the SoA.

items.title: Access to source code
items.guidance: Verify read and write access to source code, development tools and software libraries is appropriately managed. Review permissions on a sample of repositories, branch protection settings, and removal of leavers and contractors; include model code and training pipelines where they are in scope.
items.intent: Source code and development tooling are protected from unauthorized reading and change.
items.verify:
Design: Repository access rules define least privilege, limited write access and protection of production branches.
Implementation: Repository permissions are configured, SSO and MFA are enforced and branch protection is on for production branches.
Operating effectiveness: Access is reviewed, leavers and external collaborators are removed promptly and changes to protected branches require review.
items.inspect:
• Code platform members and permission levels for sample repositories
• Branch protection and required review settings on production branches
• SSO and MFA enforcement on the code platform
• Removal of leavers and external collaborators
items.questions:
• Who can push directly to production branches?
• How is access for contractors and external collaborators managed?
• How quickly are leavers removed from the code platform?
items.evidence: Code platform permission exports (e.g., GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab); branch protection settings; audit logs; SSO configuration
items.guidance_notes: Applies where the organization develops or maintains software, models or code. Confirm applicability and any exclusion justification against the SoA.

items.title: Separation of development, test and production environments
items.guidance: Verify development, test and production environments are separated and secured. Confirm environments are logically or physically separate, developer access to production is restricted and controlled, and production data is not used in test without protection (see A.8.33).
items.intent: Development and testing activity cannot harm production systems or data, because the environments are kept apart and secured.
items.verify:
Design: Environment separation rules cover separate tenants, subscriptions or accounts, access and data use.
Implementation: Environments are technically separated, and developer access to production is restricted.
Operating effectiveness: Separation is maintained, and production changes flow through controlled deployment.
items.inspect:
• Environment architecture
• Access lists for production compared with development
• Deployment pipeline controls
• Use of production data in test (links to A.8.11 and A.8.33)
items.questions:
• How are development and production separated?
• Who can access production directly?
• How does code get to production?
items.evidence: Cloud subscription or account structure; access reports; CI/CD configuration
items.guidance_notes: Applies where the organization develops or maintains software, models or code. Confirm applicability and any exclusion justification against the SoA.

items.title: Test information
items.guidance: Verify test information is appropriately selected, protected and managed. Ask whether production or client data is used for testing or model development and, if so, confirm it was authorized, protected to production standards, and deleted after use.
items.intent: Data used for testing is chosen and protected so that testing does not expose sensitive information.
items.verify:
Design: Rules for test data avoid production or sensitive data, or require approval and equivalent protection and deletion after use when it is used.
Implementation: Test data sources are documented, and approvals exist where production data is used.
Operating effectiveness: Test data is deleted after use, and test environments holding sensitive data have equivalent controls.
items.inspect:
• Test data procedure
• Sample test environments for real data
• Approvals and deletion evidence
items.questions:
• Where does test data come from?
• If real data is used in testing, who approves it, and how is it protected and removed?
items.evidence: Test data procedures; approvals; test environment access reports
items.guidance_notes: Applies where the organization develops or maintains software, models or code. Confirm applicability and any exclusion justification against the SoA.

items.title: Security testing in development and acceptance
items.guidance: Verify security testing is defined and performed in the development life cycle, and that acceptance criteria include security. Sample recent releases and confirm security tests, such as static or dynamic analysis, dependency scans or penetration tests, ran and significant findings were resolved before go-live.
items.intent: Security is tested during development and before acceptance, and failures are dealt with before release.
items.verify:
Design: Testing requirements are defined (security test cases, SAST or DAST, penetration testing for significant releases, acceptance criteria).
Implementation: Tests were run for sampled releases.
Operating effectiveness: Results are reviewed, and failures block release or require documented approval.
items.inspect:
• Test plans
• Test results for a sample release
• Penetration test for significant applications
• Acceptance sign-off
items.questions:
• What security testing is required before acceptance?
• What happens if security tests fail close to a release date?
• When was the last application penetration test?
items.evidence: Test plans and results; DAST or penetration test reports; CI pipeline logs; acceptance records
items.guidance_notes: Applies where the organization develops or maintains software, models or code. Confirm applicability and any exclusion justification against the SoA.

items.title: Outsourced development
items.guidance: Where development is outsourced, verify it is directed, monitored and reviewed against the organization's security requirements by sampling an engagement for contractual security terms and review or testing of delivered code. If no development is outsourced, confirm this and that the SoA justification reflects it.
items.intent: When development is outsourced, the organization stays in control of security outcomes by setting requirements for the provider and checking the work throughout the engagement.
items.verify:
Design: Requirements for outsourced developers are defined (contract security terms, IP, code review, testing, access).
Implementation: Contracts include the requirements, and outsourced code is reviewed and tested before acceptance.
Operating effectiveness: Provider performance is monitored, and access is removed at the end of the engagement.
items.inspect:
• List of outsourced development work
• Contracts or statements of work
• Code review or acceptance testing evidence
• Contractor access to repositories and environments
items.questions:
• Is any development outsourced?
• How is the quality and security of delivered code verified?
• How is contractor access to code and environments controlled?
items.evidence: Contracts and statements of work; acceptance test records; repository access logs
items.guidance_notes: Not applicable if no development is outsourced; confirm against the SoA.

items.title: Change management
items.guidance: Verify changes to systems and information processing facilities follow the change management procedure. Sample several recent changes, including emergency changes, and confirm each was requested, risk-assessed, approved, tested, and reviewed after implementation where required.
items.intent: Changes to systems and infrastructure are assessed, approved, tested and recorded before they are made.
items.verify:
Design: The change process defines change types (standard, normal, emergency), impact assessment, approval, testing, rollback and communication.
Implementation: Changes are recorded and approved.
Operating effectiveness: Sampled changes followed the process, emergency changes were reviewed afterwards and unauthorized changes are detected.
items.inspect:
• Change management procedure
• Sample five changes from the period, including one emergency change: request, impact, approval, testing, implementation and review
• Compare changes seen in system logs with change records to find unrecorded changes
items.questions:
• Which changes require approval, and by whom?
• How are emergency changes handled and reviewed afterwards?
• How would an unapproved change be detected?
items.evidence: Change tickets (PSA or ITSM); change advisory records; deployment logs; configuration audit logs

items.title: Contact with special interest groups
items.guidance: Verify contacts are maintained with relevant security forums, professional associations or information-sharing groups, and that they serve a purpose such as threat awareness or access to expertise. Ask who participates and for an example of information received and used. The choice of groups is the organization's.
items.intent: The security team stays connected to outside expertise, forums and advisories, so it learns about good practice and new threats early.
items.verify:
Design: Relevant sources are identified (industry information sharing groups, vendor security advisories, professional associations, government alerts).
Implementation: Staff are subscribed or are members, and information is routed to the people who can act on it.
Operating effectiveness: Information from these sources has led to action, such as patching after an advisory.
items.inspect:
• List of memberships and subscriptions and who receives them
• Examples where an advisory or forum led to a ticket, patch or configuration change
items.questions:
• Which security forums, advisories or groups does the team follow?
• Give an example of information from one of these that led to action.
• How is this information shared with the people who need it?
items.evidence: Membership records; advisory subscription lists; tickets referencing advisories; training and conference records

items.title: Threat intelligence
items.guidance: Verify threat intelligence is collected from defined sources, analyzed for relevance, and acted on. Ask for two or three recent examples where intelligence led to a control change, patch prioritization, detection rule or awareness message. Receiving feeds without analysis or action does not show the control is operating.
items.intent: Information about current threats is gathered, made relevant to the organization and used to improve prevention and detection. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Threat intelligence sources and purposes are defined and relevant to the organization's technology and sector.
Implementation: Intelligence is collected, analyzed for relevance and passed to the people who act on it.
Operating effectiveness: Intelligence demonstrably informs risk assessment, detection, patch prioritization and awareness content.
items.inspect:
• Defined sources (vendor feeds, EDR or MDR provider intelligence, CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, sector groups)
• Evidence of relevance analysis, not just forwarded emails
• Examples of resulting action: emergency patching, blocked indicators, detection tuning, risk register updates, staff alerts
• If monitoring is outsourced, what intelligence the provider applies and reports
items.questions:
• How does the organization learn about threats relevant to its technology and sector?
• Who decides whether a threat is relevant, and what happens next?
• Show a recent example where threat intelligence changed a control or a priority.
• What intelligence does your security monitoring provider apply on your behalf?
items.evidence: Threat feed subscriptions; MDR or SOC provider reports; KEV-driven patch tickets; risk register updates; security bulletins to staff

items.title: Logging
items.guidance: Verify logs of activities, exceptions, faults and other relevant events are produced, stored, protected and analyzed. Confirm which systems send logs centrally, check retention and tamper protection, and sample one log source to confirm events are actually captured.
items.intent: Systems record the events needed to detect, investigate and reconstruct what happened, and those records are protected and reviewed.
items.verify:
Design: The logging standard defines what is logged (authentication, admin activity, security events, key application events), retention and protection.
Implementation: Logging is enabled for key systems (identity provider, cloud platforms, EDR, firewalls, servers, SaaS audit logs) and centralized where appropriate.
Operating effectiveness: Logs are protected from tampering, retention meets requirements and logs are actually used.
items.inspect:
• Logging standard
• Audit logging enabled on key platforms (e.g., Microsoft 365 unified audit log)
• Log sources feeding the SIEM or MDR compared with the list of critical systems
• Retention settings
• Who can delete or alter logs
items.questions:
• Which systems send logs to central monitoring?
• How long are logs kept?
• Who can delete or alter logs?
items.evidence: Logging standard; SIEM or MDR log source list; audit log configuration; retention settings

items.title: Clock synchronization
items.guidance: Verify system clocks are synchronized to approved time sources so events can be correlated across systems. Check time source settings on a sample of servers, network devices and cloud services, and compare timestamps across two log sources for consistency.
items.intent: System clocks agree with a trusted time source, so logs from different systems can be lined up.
items.verify:
Design: An approved time source is defined.
Implementation: Systems are configured to synchronize (domain, NTP, cloud platform defaults).
Operating effectiveness: Timestamps line up across log sources, which matters for investigations.
items.inspect:
• NTP configuration on network devices and servers
• Compare timestamps of one event across two log sources
items.questions:
• What time source do systems use?
• Would firewall, EDR and identity provider timestamps line up in an investigation?
items.evidence: NTP configuration; device configurations; log samples

items.title: Monitoring activities
items.guidance: Verify networks, systems and applications are monitored for anomalous behavior and that potential incidents are evaluated and acted on. Review how alerts are generated and triaged, for example through a SIEM, MDR or SOC service, sample recent alerts, and confirm response times meet the organization's expectations.
items.intent: Unusual behavior on networks, systems and applications is spotted and looked into, so incidents are caught early. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: Monitoring scope, detection use cases and responsibilities (internal or MDR or SOC provider) are defined, including coverage outside business hours.
Implementation: Monitoring operates across in-scope systems, and alerts reach responders.
Operating effectiveness: Alerts are triaged promptly, detections are tuned and coverage gaps are closed.
items.inspect:
• Monitoring provider scope compared with the critical systems list
• Sample alerts and response times
• Monthly service reports
• Escalation contacts are current
• Tuning records
items.questions:
• What does the monitoring service watch, and what does it not watch?
• How quickly are high-severity alerts responded to?
• What is the escalation path outside business hours?
items.evidence: MDR or SOC contract and reports; SIEM alert rules; alert tickets; escalation matrix

items.title: Information security incident management planning and preparation
items.guidance: Verify an incident management plan defines roles, procedures, communication and escalation, and that the people named know their part. Check whether the plan has been tested, for example through a tabletop exercise, and whether lessons from the test were used.
items.intent: The organization is ready for incidents before they happen: the plan, roles, contacts and tools are in place and people know them.
items.verify:
Design: The incident response plan defines roles, classification, escalation, communication and links to legal and contractual notification.
Implementation: Roles are assigned to named people (including external parties such as an MDR provider, legal counsel and forensics), contact lists are current and tools are available.
Operating effectiveness: The plan is tested through exercises or real incidents and updated from what was learned.
items.inspect:
• Incident Response Plan: version, approval, named roles and escalation paths
• Spot-check two contacts in the contact list
• Most recent tabletop or test: date, scenario, participants, improvement actions and their status
• Alignment with the MDR or SOC provider's escalation procedures
items.questions:
• Who can declare an incident?
• How would an employee report a suspected incident?
• Who participates in incident response, including external parties?
• When was the process last tested?
• What changed based on the most recent test or incident?
items.evidence: Incident Response Plan and playbooks; contact lists; tabletop exercise reports; MDR or SOC service description; legal, forensics or cyber insurance retainers

items.title: Information security event reporting
items.guidance: Verify staff know how and where to report observed or suspected security events promptly, and that the reporting channel works. Ask a sample of staff how they would report a phishing email or lost device, and confirm recent reports were received and handled through the defined channel.
items.intent: Anyone who sees something suspicious knows how to report it quickly, and does so.
items.verify:
Design: Reporting channels are defined and simple (report-phish button, help desk, security mailbox), including for contractors.
Implementation: Channels are communicated to staff and work.
Operating effectiveness: Staff actually report events, reports are triaged promptly and reporters receive feedback.
items.inspect:
• Reporting channels and how they are communicated
• Recent reports and response times, or a test of the channel agreed in advance
• Volume and trend of user reports (e.g., report-phish submissions)
• Ask staff how they would report an event
items.questions:
• (To staff) How would you report a suspicious email or a lost laptop?
• What happens after a report is submitted?
• How many events did staff report this year, and is the number going up or down?
items.evidence: Incident reporting procedure; report-phish add-in statistics; help desk tickets; security mailbox; awareness materials

items.title: Assessment and decision on information security events
items.guidance: Verify security events are assessed against defined criteria to decide whether they are incidents, and that the decision and rationale are recorded. Sample several events from the ticketing or monitoring system and confirm they were categorized and prioritized consistently.
items.intent: Security events are triaged consistently, so real incidents are recognized and escalated and false alarms are closed with a reason.
items.verify:
Design: Criteria for declaring an incident and severity levels are defined.
Implementation: Events are triaged against the criteria by assigned people or the monitoring provider.
Operating effectiveness: Decisions are recorded and consistent, and no events are left unassessed.
items.inspect:
• Incident classification criteria or severity matrix
• Sample five security events (EDR alerts, MDR tickets, user reports): decision recorded, timeliness and consistency with the criteria
• Events escalated to incidents and events closed as false positives, with rationale
items.questions:
• What makes an event an incident here?
• Who performs triage outside business hours?
• Show me an event that was closed as not an incident, and explain why.
