items.evidence: Severity matrix; MDR or SOC tickets; EDR alert console; ticketing system; incident log

items.title: Response to information security incidents
items.guidance: Sample recent incidents and verify the response followed the documented procedures, including containment, escalation, communication, recovery and closure. Check timelines for delays and confirm notifications required by the plan or by contract were made.
items.intent: When an incident happens, the response follows the organization's documented approach, including containment, recovery and any required notification.
items.verify:
Design: Response procedures or playbooks exist for likely scenarios (ransomware, business email compromise, lost device, data exposure).
Implementation: Actual incidents followed the procedures through containment, eradication, recovery, communication and notification decisions.
Operating effectiveness: Response was timely, notifications met legal and contractual deadlines, and records are complete.
items.inspect:
• Incident log for the audit period
• Sample one to three incidents (or the most recent exercise if there were none): timeline against the plan, containment actions, notification decisions and timing
• Notification decisions compared with legal and contractual requirements
items.questions:
• Walk me through the most significant incident this year.
• How was the decision to notify, or not notify, clients or regulators made?
• Which playbook steps were hard to follow in practice?
items.evidence: Incident tickets and reports; incident timelines; communication and notification records; MDR or SOC incident reports

items.title: Contact with authorities
items.guidance: Verify the organization knows which authorities to contact (for example law enforcement or regulators) and in what circumstances, and that contact details and responsibilities are current. Check the incident response plan for notification triggers and confirm the contact list was reviewed recently.
items.intent: The organization can reach the right regulators, law enforcement and other authorities quickly when a situation requires it.
items.verify:
Design: Relevant authorities and the conditions for contacting them are identified (e.g., breach notification obligations, law enforcement, national cyber agencies).
Implementation: Current contact details and the people authorized to make contact are documented and reachable during an incident.
Operating effectiveness: Contact details are verified periodically, and any required contact in the period was timely.
items.inspect:
• Authority contact list: who, when to contact, who is authorized, and when it was last verified
• Link to the incident response plan and to breach notification requirements (e.g., applicable state breach notification statutes and contractual notification duties)
• Any contact with authorities during the period and its timeliness
items.questions:
• Under what circumstances would you notify a regulator or law enforcement?
• Who is authorized to make that contact?
• When were these contact details last checked?
items.evidence: Incident Response Plan contact appendix; authority contact list; breach notification procedure; records of any notifications made

items.title: Collection of evidence
items.guidance: Verify procedures exist for identifying, collecting, preserving and handling evidence from security events so it can be relied on if disciplinary or legal action follows. Ask who is authorized to collect evidence and how chain of custody and log preservation are handled; if no incident has needed it, test readiness by walkthrough.
items.intent: Evidence from security events is gathered and preserved so it remains usable for investigation, disciplinary, legal or insurance purposes.
items.verify:
Design: Evidence handling procedures exist (chain of custody, log preservation, forensic imaging, legal hold), with roles including any external forensics provider.
Implementation: Tools and retainers are in place, and log retention supports investigations.
Operating effectiveness: When evidence was needed, it was preserved properly.
items.inspect:
• Evidence collection procedure and chain-of-custody form
• Forensics retainer or the monitoring provider's evidence-handling capability
• Log retention periods compared with investigation needs
• Evidence records from any incident that required investigation
items.questions:
• If a device were involved in a serious incident, how would evidence be preserved?
• Who would perform forensic collection?
• How long are logs kept, and is that long enough to investigate an incident discovered late?
items.evidence: Evidence handling procedure; chain-of-custody forms; forensics retainer; log retention settings; legal hold procedure

items.title: Learning from information security incidents
items.guidance: Verify knowledge gained from incidents is used to strengthen controls. Ask for examples where an incident led to a change in controls, procedures, training or the risk assessment, and confirm post-incident reviews are held for significant incidents.
items.intent: Each significant incident leaves the organization stronger because lessons are captured and acted on.
items.verify:
Design: Post-incident review is required for defined severities.
Implementation: Lessons-learned reviews are held and actions assigned.
Operating effectiveness: Actions are completed and reduce recurrence, and incident trends are analyzed.
items.inspect:
• Post-incident review records for significant incidents
• Resulting actions: owner, due date, status and evidence of completion
• Incident trend reporting to management (links to 9.1 and 9.3)
• Repeat incidents of the same type
items.questions:
• What changed because of the last significant incident?
• Who tracks lessons-learned actions to completion?
• Are there recurring incident types, and what is being done about them?
items.evidence: Post-incident review reports; corrective action records in the controlled document repository; risk register updates; incident trend reports

items.title: Information backup
items.guidance: Verify backups of information, software and systems are taken and tested in line with the organization's backup policy. Check backup job reports for success and coverage of key systems and SaaS data, and review the most recent restore test to confirm data can actually be recovered.
items.intent: Backup copies of information, software and systems are kept in line with the organization's backup requirements, and restores are tested so recovery can be relied on.
items.verify:
Design: Backup requirements (scope, frequency, retention, protection and restore testing) are defined and aligned with recovery needs, including SaaS data such as Microsoft 365 where relevant.
Implementation: Required systems and data are included in backup jobs whose schedules match the requirements, and backup data is protected (encryption, immutability or segregation).
Operating effectiveness: Backup jobs are monitored, failures are addressed, retention is appropriate, and restoration capability is periodically validated.
items.inspect:
• Documented backup requirements
• Backup console and configuration: compare protected systems with the list of required systems
• Recent job results and failure alerts
• Retention configuration
• Restore-test documentation
• Applicable recovery requirements (RPO and RTO from the business impact analysis)
items.questions:
• What systems are required to be backed up?
• Who monitors failed backups?
• What happens when a backup fails?
• When was the last successful restore test?
• Does the implemented backup schedule align with documented RPO expectations?
items.evidence: Backup policy or standard; backup console and job reports; failure alert tickets; restore test records; business impact analysis

items.title: Redundancy of information processing facilities
items.guidance: Verify information processing facilities have enough redundancy to meet availability requirements. Identify key systems and their availability targets, confirm redundancy exists, such as multi-zone hosting or failover, and check whether failover has been tested.
items.intent: Critical services keep running through the failure of a component because enough redundancy was built in to meet availability needs.
items.verify:
Design: Availability requirements come from the business impact analysis, and redundancy is designed for critical components (cloud zones or regions, network, identity, key SaaS).
Implementation: Redundancy is implemented as designed.
Operating effectiveness: Failover is tested, and single points of failure are identified and addressed or accepted.
items.inspect:
• Architecture diagrams for critical services
• Redundancy configuration (availability zones, replication, secondary internet)
• Failover test results
• Documented single points of failure
items.questions:
• What single points of failure exist for critical services?
• When was failover last tested?
• Does redundancy support the recovery times in the business impact analysis?
items.evidence: Architecture diagrams; cloud configuration; failover test records; business impact analysis

items.title: Capacity management
items.guidance: Verify resource use is monitored and adjusted to current and expected capacity needs. Review capacity monitoring or alerting for key systems and cloud services, and ask for an example where a capacity issue was anticipated or resolved. The planning approach should be proportionate to the environment.
items.intent: Systems have enough capacity for today's workload and planned growth, so performance and availability are not put at risk.
items.verify:
Design: Capacity monitoring is defined for critical systems (compute, storage, licenses, bandwidth, cloud quotas).
Implementation: Monitoring and alerting are configured.
Operating effectiveness: Alerts are acted on, and capacity planning considers growth such as new client workloads.
items.inspect:
• Monitoring dashboards and alert thresholds for storage, compute, cloud quotas and spend
• Recent capacity alerts and the actions taken
• Capacity planning notes for new projects
items.questions:
• How would you know a critical system is running out of capacity?
• Show a recent capacity alert and what was done about it.
• How is capacity planned for new projects?
items.evidence: RMM and cloud monitoring dashboards; alert tickets; cloud cost and quota reports; capacity plans

items.title: ICT readiness for business continuity
items.guidance: Verify ICT readiness is planned, implemented, maintained and tested against business continuity objectives, with defined recovery time and recovery point targets for key systems. Review the most recent recovery or failover test and confirm results met the targets or gaps were addressed.
items.intent: Critical ICT services can be recovered within the time and data-loss limits the business needs, and this is proven by testing rather than assumed. New in the 2022 edition.
items.verify:
Design: The business impact analysis sets recovery time and recovery point objectives for critical services, and ICT continuity strategies are designed to meet them.
Implementation: Recovery capabilities (backups, redundancy, alternate sites, recovery runbooks) are in place for critical systems.
Operating effectiveness: Recovery tests show recovery within the objectives, and gaps are remediated.
items.inspect:
• Business impact analysis: critical services with RTO and RPO
• Recovery runbooks for critical systems
• Most recent recovery test: scope, achieved recovery time and point against targets, issues and remediation
• Backup and replication settings compared with the RPO (links to A.8.13 and A.8.14)
items.questions:
• Which systems are most critical, and what are their recovery targets?
• When was recovery last tested, and did it meet the targets?
• What failed or took longer than expected in the last test?
items.evidence: Business impact analysis; BCDR Policy and Plan; recovery runbooks; recovery test reports; backup and replication configuration

items.title: Information security during disruption
items.guidance: Verify the organization has planned how to keep information security at an appropriate level during disruption, not only how to restore operations. Review continuity or crisis plans for security considerations such as emergency access, alternate working arrangements and data protection during recovery, and check whether these were exercised.
items.intent: Information security does not lapse when normal operations are disrupted: the organization has worked out in advance which protections must continue, and how, during an outage, crisis or recovery.
items.verify:
Design: Continuity and recovery plans address security during disruption (alternate environments, emergency access, manual workarounds, surges in remote work).
Implementation: Security controls for recovery environments and alternate processes are defined.
Operating effectiveness: Exercises confirm that security is maintained during disruption (e.g., the recovery environment has equivalent access control, logging and endpoint protection).
items.inspect:
• BCDR plan sections on security during disruption
• Emergency (break-glass) access procedure and how its use is monitored
• Test or exercise records: were security controls validated in the recovery scenario?
items.questions:
• If the primary environment were unavailable, how would access control and monitoring work in the recovery environment?
• How is emergency access controlled and reviewed?
• Were security controls checked during the last continuity test?
items.evidence: BCDR Policy and Plan; break-glass account procedure and sign-in logs; continuity and recovery test reports

items.title: Monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation
items.guidance: Verify the organization has decided what to monitor and measure, the methods, frequency, and who analyzes and evaluates the results for ISMS performance and effectiveness. Sample two or three metrics and confirm the data is collected as defined, and that results are reported and acted on. The choice of metrics is the organization's; the standard requires documented information as evidence of the results.
items.intent: The organization measures what matters for information security, in ways that give consistent and repeatable results, and uses the results to judge how well the ISMS is performing.
items.verify:
Design: A defined set of measures exists, each with a method, frequency and responsibility for measurement and analysis.
Implementation: Measures are collected as defined, and results are retained.
Operating effectiveness: Results are analyzed, reported to management and acted on when performance falls short.
items.inspect:
• Definitions of metrics and their data sources
• Two or three recent metric reports
• Re-compute one metric from source data to test reproducibility
• Evidence of analysis and the decisions it produced
items.questions:
• What does the organization measure to know whether the ISMS is working?
• Who analyzes the results, and what happens when a metric misses its target?
• Can you show me the source data behind this metric?
items.evidence: Metric definitions; dashboards; security reports (patch compliance, EDR, vulnerability, training completion); management review inputs

items.title: Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security
items.guidance: Verify managers and control owners regularly check compliance with security policies, rules and standards in their areas, and that non-compliance is recorded and addressed. Ask for recent compliance checks, such as configuration compliance reports, access review results or policy compliance reviews.
items.intent: The organization checks regularly that its security policies and standards are actually followed, and fixes the gaps it finds.
items.verify:
Design: Owners are responsible for reviewing compliance in their areas, and technical compliance checks are defined.
Implementation: Compliance reviews and technical checks take place (configuration compliance reports, manager reviews).
Operating effectiveness: Noncompliance is identified, its cause understood and corrected.
items.inspect:
• Evidence of compliance checks (configuration compliance dashboards, periodic owner reviews)
• A sample of noncompliance that was identified and how it was resolved
• Technical compliance tooling (e.g., MDM compliance policies, Secure Score) and remediation tracking
items.questions:
• Between audits, how do you know people and systems comply with policy?
• What noncompliance was found recently, and how was it resolved?
• Who reviews technical compliance reports?
items.evidence: Compliance reports; MDM compliance dashboards; configuration baseline reports; corrective action records

items.title: Independent review of information security
items.guidance: Verify the organization's approach to information security is independently reviewed at planned intervals or after significant change, by people independent of the area reviewed. Review the most recent one, such as an external assessment or certification audit, and confirm results were reported and acted on. This program contributes to the control, so auditor objectivity matters here.
items.intent: Someone independent of the day-to-day work periodically checks how information security is managed, especially after significant change.
items.verify:
Design: Independent reviews are planned (internal audit by independent auditors, external assessments, penetration tests, certification audits).
Implementation: Reviews were performed by people independent of the area reviewed.
Operating effectiveness: Results were reported to management and acted on.
items.inspect:
• Schedule of independent reviews for the period
• Independence of reviewers from the areas they reviewed
• Reporting of results to management and the resulting actions
items.questions:
• What independent reviews of information security took place this year?
• How was reviewer independence ensured?
• What changed as a result?
items.evidence: This workbook; internal audit reports; certification audit reports; penetration test reports; management review minutes
items.guidance_notes: This internal audit program contributes to this control, so auditor objectivity (procedure Section 7) is directly relevant here.

items.title: Internal audit (general)
items.guidance: Review the previous cycle's internal audit reports and verify they reach a clear conclusion on both conformity (to the organization's own requirements and ISO/IEC 27001) and effective implementation, and that audits occurred at the planned intervals. Because this item audits the audit process itself, it must be reviewed by someone other than the program owner.
items.intent: Planned internal audits tell the organization whether the ISMS meets its own requirements and ISO/IEC 27001, and whether it is working and being maintained.
items.verify:
Design: The internal audit procedure defines audits that test both conformity (organizational and ISO requirements) and effectiveness.
Implementation: Audits were performed at the planned intervals.
Operating effectiveness: Audits tested effectiveness with records, samples and observation, not only document existence, and produced useful information for management.
items.inspect:
• Annual Audit Program and Dashboard: was each quarterly package completed by the end of its quarter?
• Audit reports in the controlled document repository: criteria cover both ISO/IEC 27001 and organizational requirements
• Workpapers showing samples, records and walkthroughs, not only policy review
items.questions:
• Were all quarterly packages completed within their quarters? If not, why, and who approved the change?
• How do audits test whether controls work, not only whether they are documented?
items.evidence: ISMS Internal Audit Procedure; the audit program; audit reports and workpapers in the controlled document repository

items.title: Internal audit programme
items.guidance: Verify the audit program defines frequency, methods, responsibilities, planning and reporting, and that each audit had defined criteria and scope, objective and impartial auditors, and results reported to relevant management. Compare the planned quarterly packages with completed audits and the the controlled document repository audit records to confirm the program is followed in practice. The standard requires documented information as evidence of program implementation and audit results.
items.intent: A planned audit program sets how often, how and by whom audits are done and reported, taking account of how important each process is and what earlier audits found. Each audit has a defined scope and criteria, auditors are objective and impartial, results reach relevant management, and records show the program ran.
items.verify:
Design: The program defines frequency, methods, responsibilities, planning and reporting, and considers process importance and previous results.
Implementation: Each audit has a defined scope and criteria and an objective auditor; results were reported to management; records are retained.
Operating effectiveness: The program is followed and updated based on results and changes, and full coverage of the applicable ISMS is achieved within the cycle.
items.inspect:
• Annual Audit Program tab: the four quarterly packages with auditor, status, progress and deadline; scope is the set of items in each quarterly worksheet, and criteria are defined in the procedure
• Dashboard coverage figures and the reasons for any gaps
• Auditor objectivity and impartiality for each audit (no auditor was the sole validator of their own work; procedure Section 7)
• Evidence audit results were reported to management (report distribution, management review inputs)
• Program changes made in response to previous results
items.questions:
• How were the quarterly groupings and their sequence decided?
• How is auditor objectivity ensured for areas the auditor helps to operate or document?
• How, and to whom, are audit results reported?
• How did previous audit results change this program?
items.evidence: This workbook; ISMS Internal Audit Procedure; the controlled document repository audit records; management review minutes; auditor assignment and competence records

items.title: Protection of information systems during audit testing
items.guidance: Verify audit tests and assurance activities on operational systems are planned and agreed between the tester and appropriate management. Review how recent penetration tests or audit access were scoped and authorized, and confirm this program uses read-only, time-limited access when reviewing live configurations.
items.intent: Audits and technical tests of live systems are agreed in advance and carried out without disrupting operations or exposing information.
items.verify:
Design: Rules for audit and testing activities cover scope, read-only access, timing, approvals and rules of engagement for penetration tests.
Implementation: Audits and penetration tests had agreed scope and approval, and auditor access was read-only and time-limited.
Operating effectiveness: Temporary audit access was removed afterwards, and testing caused no disruption.
items.inspect:
• Penetration test rules of engagement and authorization
• Internal audit access requests
• Removal of temporary auditor access
items.questions:
• How are penetration tests authorized and scoped?
• What access do auditors receive, and when is it removed?
• Did any testing cause disruption?
items.evidence: Rules of engagement; authorization letters; temporary access tickets; test reports
items.guidance_notes: Also applies to this internal audit program: request read-only, time-limited access when reviewing live configurations.

items.title: Management review (general)
items.guidance: Verify management reviews were held at the planned intervals with top management participating. Review dates, attendees and agendas for the most recent reviews. The interval is set by the organization, so confirm it is defined and was met.
items.intent: Top management periodically steps back to confirm the ISMS is still suitable, adequate and effective.
items.verify:
Design: The planned interval for management review is defined.
Implementation: Reviews were held at that interval with top management taking part.
Operating effectiveness: Reviews are substantive, producing decisions rather than simply noting reports.
items.inspect:
• Management review schedule and minutes for the period
• Attendance by top management
• Interval between reviews compared with the defined frequency
items.questions:
• How often is management review held, and who attends?
• What was the most significant decision from the last review?
items.evidence: Management review agendas, minutes, attendance and presentation materials

items.title: Management review inputs
items.guidance: Compare the latest management review agenda and minutes with the inputs the standard lists, and confirm each was covered with real content, including status of prior actions, changes in issues and in interested party needs (added in the 2022 edition), performance trends, audit results, risk status and improvement opportunities. Missing or placeholder inputs are the common gap.
items.intent: Management review is fed the information it needs: follow-up on earlier decisions, changes in context and stakeholder expectations, performance trends (nonconformities, measurements, audit results, objectives), stakeholder feedback, risk status and improvement opportunities.
items.verify:
Design: The management review agenda or template covers every required input.
Implementation: Each input was actually presented at the reviews held in the period.
Operating effectiveness: Inputs are current and specific enough to support decisions, and internal audit results appear as an input.
items.inspect:
• Compare the agenda and minutes of the last review against each required input, including changes in interested parties' needs (added in 2022)
• Confirm internal audit results and program status were presented
• Check that inputs were current (not last year's figures)
items.questions:
• How is the management review agenda built?
• Where did the internal audit results appear in the last review?
• Which input led to the most discussion or action?
items.evidence: Management review input pack; minutes; dashboards and reports presented

items.title: Management review results
items.guidance: Verify management review outputs record decisions on improvement opportunities and any needed changes to the ISMS, and that each decision has an owner and is tracked. Trace two or three decisions from the latest minutes to confirm follow-through. The standard requires documented information as evidence of management review results.
items.intent: Management review ends in recorded decisions on improvement and on any changes the ISMS needs.
items.verify:
Design: Management review outputs are recorded as decisions and actions.
Implementation: Decisions and actions have owners and dates.
Operating effectiveness: Actions are followed up and closed, and resulting ISMS changes are made.
items.inspect:
• Decisions and actions from the last review, with owners and due dates
• Follow-up of those actions at the next review
• ISMS changes that resulted from review decisions
items.questions:
• What decisions came out of the last management review?
• How are the resulting actions tracked?
• Which actions are still open, and why?
items.evidence: Management review minutes and action list; related change or project records

items.title: Nonconformity and corrective action
items.guidance: Sample open and closed nonconformities and verify each shows the immediate reaction, root cause analysis, actions taken, a check for similar issues elsewhere, and a review of effectiveness. Check that actions were proportionate to the effect of the nonconformity and that ISMS changes were made where needed. The standard requires documented information on nonconformities, actions and results.
items.intent: When a requirement is not met, the organization contains and fixes the problem, finds out why it happened and whether it could happen elsewhere, acts on the cause, confirms the action worked and keeps records.
items.verify:
Design: A corrective action process defines how nonconformities are recorded, analyzed, corrected and verified.
Implementation: Nonconformities from internal audits, certification audits and incidents are recorded with root cause and actions.
Operating effectiveness: Actions are completed, their effectiveness is verified, and similar issues elsewhere were considered.
items.inspect:
• Corrective action records in the controlled document repository: nonconformity, correction, root cause, action, effectiveness review
• Sample nonconformities from internal audit, certification audit and incidents
• Evidence that the organization checked whether similar nonconformities exist elsewhere
• Effectiveness verification performed by someone other than the person who implemented the action, where practical
items.questions:
• Walk me through a recent nonconformity from detection to closure.
• How was the root cause determined?
• How, and by whom, was effectiveness verified?
• Did you check whether the same problem existed elsewhere?
items.evidence: Corrective action records (the controlled document repository); certification body audit reports; incident post-incident reviews; root cause analyses

items.title: Continual improvement
items.guidance: Ask for examples of ISMS improvements made in the past year from sources such as audits, incidents, metrics, management review or staff suggestions, and verify improvement is ongoing rather than limited to responding to certification findings. ISO does not require a separate improvement register; judge on evidence of improvements actually made.
items.intent: The ISMS gets better over time at fitting the organization, covering what it needs to and delivering results.
items.verify:
Design: Sources of improvement are identified (audits, incidents, metrics, management review, staff suggestions).
Implementation: Improvements are implemented.
Operating effectiveness: Improvement is demonstrable over time through better metrics, fewer repeat issues or stronger controls.
items.inspect:
• Examples of improvements made in the period and their origin
• Metric trends over time
• Repeat nonconformities or repeat incidents that suggest improvement is not happening
items.questions:
• What improved in the ISMS over the past year, and how do you know?
• Where do improvement ideas come from?
items.evidence: Improvement records; management review decisions; corrective action records; project records; metric trends
